Folate receptor alpha (FOLRa), a protein overexpressed on the surface of breast cancer cells, represents an attractive therapeutic target for this approach. Previously, gold nanoparticles functionalized with folic acid (FA) have been shown to selectively bind to FOLRa-overexpressing cells, however the molecular architecture linking FA to the nanoparticle surface represents a critical design tradeoff. Traditional linear polyethylene glycol (PEG) linkers, the current standard for FA conjugation, may shroud targeting capability of FA through steric interactions at longer lengths. However, shorter linker lengths cause rapid deterioration of nanoparticle stability. Peptoids, a synthetic, biomimetic polymer with tunable side chain chemistry, offer a promising alternative linker architecture which may help retain targeting efficiency without compromising nanoparticle stability through their brush-like structure. To investigate how linker architecture influences targeting, gold nanoparticles were functionalized with FA using both linear PEG and peptoid linkers and evaluated for their interactions with FOLRa-overexpressing cancer cells. Initial results suggest that linker architecture meaningfully affects cellular interactions, pointing to peptoids as a possible alternative to retaining targeting efficacy and without compromising stability of targeted nanoparticle-based cancer therapy. Ongoing work focuses on detailed material characterization to elucidate the underlying chemical mechanisms responsible for these differences.

title: "Why don't fidget toys work?": Embodied artifacts in a MS summer camp.
abstract: In the Hubspace Summer Program, Evanston middle schoolers of color spend 6 weeks learning about STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, and Mathematics) and telling/listening to stories, within an environment that blends joy and learning. Educators, including Dr. Shirin Vossoughi and myself, are also researchers, documenting then analyzing the program to redesign it for the next summer and share knowledge with the broader field. This style of educational research, when done with care and rooted in relationships, can unearth understandings central for educators' and young people's growth. As an Emerging Scholar, I took ethnographic field notes, recorded the video and audio of pedagogical interactions, and began my educator journey. After the summer, I conducted interviews with educators, coded field notes to see the connections between various forms of movement and focus among campers, and co-designed a week of the summer 2026 program. Watching my fellow Hubspace educators, I noticed how they saw the body as integral to learning, giving campers the freedom to move while thinking (e.g. crocheting while listening to an educator or friend). Over the school year, I read through fieldnotes and interviewed fellow educators to understand how and why they approached learning this way. They described their unique ways of understanding focus and learning that help them honor our young people's bodies and minds. While redesigning the curriculum for next summer, we incorporated new strategies such as drawing as an intentional form of storylistening, and aim to understand how these are taken up by the campers.

title: Evaluating Reliance on Misinformation for Video Stimuli
abstract: The continued influence effect (CIE) is the cognitive psychological phenomenon where people continue to rely upon or mention information that has been retracted. Previous research indicates that providing participants with a plausible alternative explanation for retracted information reduces CIEs, in contrast to when an alternative explanation is not provided. This alternative explanation may fill any related mental model gap when a cause is refuted. However, this issue has predominantly been studied using text stimuli. It remains unclear whether and how other kinds of media might lead to CIEs. This study uses a fictional news broadcast about a chemical spell to test if CIEs can be applied to video stimuli. Participants were first prompted to watch one of four fictional broadcasts: a broadcast with no relevant information, a broadcast where a causal explanation is not discounted, a broadcast with a causal explanation that is discounted, and a broadcast with a causal explanation that is discounted and corrected with an alternative cause. They were then prompted to answer open-ended questions about the events of the story. Inference scores and endorsements are calculated by using the numbering of references that participants make to the original cause in both the open-response memory, inference, and free-recall questions. Reliance on CIEs will then be assessed based on inference scores and endorsement of the original cause. This survey is in the process of being administered, and responses have not yet been recorded.

title: Ingredients of Our Black Hole's Diet: Correlating Different Gas Phases in the Center of the Milky Way
abstract: At the center of our Milky Way sits Sagittarius A\* (Sgr A\*), a supermassive black hole four million times the mass of our Sun, and our closest cosmic laboratory for understanding how black holes grow and the fate of our galaxy. Despite the Galactic Center being the best resolved region around any supermassive black hole, we still don't fully understand how gas ends up feeding Sgr A\* versus being pushed away from it-a gap that limits our understanding of black hole growth across the universe. Using radio telescope observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and machine learning techniques, we map two distinct phases of gas near Sgr A\*, cold molecular gas and hot ionized hydrogen. These techniques isolate dominant signals in the complex, three-dimensional data and statistically group gas structures by their properties. We identify several distinct gas structures near Sgr A\*, including bow shocks and expanding shells, each shedding light on a different stage of black hole activity. This work is ongoing, and our continued analysis aims at understanding how these structures connect to the cycle of black hole feeding and feedback in our galaxy.

title: shRNA-Mediated Knockdown of SPTLC3 Impairs Epidermal Differentiation and Filaggrin Expression in 3D Skin Organoid Models
abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD), commonly known as eczema, is a chronic condition that affects more than 200 million people worldwide. It often causes dry, itchy, and inflamed skin because the skin barrier does not work properly. A healthy skin barrier depends on ceramides, natural fats that help the skin hold moisture and block irritants. SPTLC3 is part of an enzyme that helps make ceramides, but its exact role in skin health is not fully understood. This study examined whether lower levels of SPTLC3 may contribute to the skin barrier problems seen in eczema. To test this, we reduced SPTLC3 levels in human skin cells called keratinocytes using shRNA, a tool that lowers gene activity. These cells were grown in three-dimensional (3D) skin organoids, which are lab-grown models that closely resemble real human skin. We then measured changes in important skin barrier genes and proteins using molecular imaging and gene analysis techniques. When SPTLC3 was reduced, levels of filaggrin also decreased. Filaggrin is a key protein that helps skin stay strong, hydrated, and protected. We also observed changes in other markers involved in normal skin development, suggesting the skin tissue was not maturing properly. Overall, our findings suggest that SPTLC3 plays an important role in keeping the skin barrier healthy. Lower SPTLC3 levels may weaken the skin and contribute to eczema. Understanding this pathway could help researchers develop new treatments that repair the skin barrier and improve symptoms for people with atopic dermatitis.

title: Optimization of an inducible genetic strategy to study olfactory monoallelic expression
abstract: Olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs), responsible for detecting smells, each express only one odorant receptor (OR) gene chosen from thousands of possible options. However, the biological mechanisms that control this “one neuron–one receptor” rule are poorly understood. These neurons are continuously generated from stem cells in the olfactory epithelium, and receptor choice occurs during a short developmental window in immature OSNs. Studying this process requires the ability to control gene activity before this critical window. To do this, we used a genetic system in which the drug tamoxifen turns genes on/off in developing neurons. This system relies on an enzyme (Cre recombinase) expressed from the Ascl1 locus in stem cells. A key challenge is ensuring that this system activates efficiently in the right cells. To optimize this, we used a fluorescent reporter (Ai14; ROSA-tdTomato) that marks recombined cells, and tested different conditions by varying (1) the age at which tamoxifen was administered and (2) the number of consecutive treatment days. We measured recombination using imaging and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). We found that earlier treatment, starting at postnatal day 2 (P2), produced the highest proportion of labeled neurons, while later treatment resulted in more total labeled neurons due to overall tissue growth. The optimal balance was achieved at P5. Changing the number of treatment days (1, 3, or 5) did not significantly affect labeling. These results establish an optimized method for controlling gene activity in developing olfactory neurons, providing a foundation for studying how neurons select a single receptor gene.

title: Rupture Instabilities of Thin Colloidal Films
abstract: Thin liquid films, which have a thickness ranging from a fraction of a nanometer to micrometers, have applications across various fields including disease transmission, industrial coating, and biomedical devices. Liquid films are a convenient system for studying fluid dynamics in two dimensions. This project focuses on films made with colloidal suspensions, which are formed when micron-sized particles, called colloids, are suspended in the film. When the concentration of colloids in the liquid is high enough, colloidal suspensions exhibit non-Newtonian behavior, which means that the liquid flow direction changes when force is applied. Examples of Newtonian fluids are water and oil, whereas some non-Newtonian fluids are mucus, paint, and oobleck. These colloidal films have been shown to exhibit various instabilities during rupture that qualitatively deviate from the expectation for Newtonian film rupture. To study this behavior, colloidal films across a range of thicknesses and colloidal concentrations were recorded during spontaneous and induced rupture on a high speed camera, and then analyzed using ImageJ and Python. The films are formed with a flat horizontal film stretcher and experiments are performed in a sealed box so that humidity can be stabilized and environmental factors can be mitigated. Analysis of the films is on-going, but it has been found that different colloid geometry (rods or spheres) corresponds to different instabilities, and there appears to be a critical transition thickness between types of instabilities. Further exploration is being done into the dependence of the speed of the rupture on thickness, colloidal concentration, and colloidal geometry.

title: Liposomal Spherical Nucleic Acid (LSNA) for the Treatment of Inflammation
abstract: Chronic inflammatory diseases arise when immune activation and inflammation are dysregulated. Common drug therapies, such as steroids, effectively reduce acute inflammation, but bring severe side effects with long-term or high-dose usage. To this end, recent studies have suggested that inhibitory oligonucleotides (INH-ODNs) can serve as alternative therapies by inhibiting the initial activation of inflammatory responses and preventing symptoms from spreading. These molecules bind to and inhibit the activation of a target immune receptor with high specificity, making them an ideal candidate for dysfunctional immune system signaling. However, nucleic acids are susceptible to rapid nuclease degradation and have poor cellular uptake, limiting their translation into clinical treatments. To address these challenges, we employ liposomal spherical nucleic acid (LSNA) nanoparticles for the delivery of INH18, an INH-ODN, to investigate the hypothesis that a liposomal structure can act as an effective scaffold to improve nucleic acid uptake and delivery. We first construct an amphiphilic conjugate where 3'-disulfide-INH18 was conjugated to a phospholipid via a stable maleimide linker. This amphiphilic conjugate was then anchored into a DOPC liposomal core to form the desired LSNA. This LSNA treatment was tested against stimulated inflammation in an inflammation-reporter cell line, measuring the production of the reporter protein. Inflammatory cytokine production was also evaluated using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs).Our results indicate that the INH18 LSNA can effectively suppress both CpG-induced activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, laying the groundwork for synergistic dual-therapy strategies that combine upstream receptor inhibition by INH-ODNs with the downstream alleviation of inflammation by steroids.

title: Earth System History Repeats Itself: Contextualizing our Current Situation Through Records of Ancient Volcanism and Acidification
abstract: Ocean acidification is a dangerous consequence of heightened carbon emissions. When the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere increases, more carbon dioxide is absorbed by the ocean, where it reacts with water molecules to ultimately increase marine acidity and negatively impact marine ecosystems. One way to understand the longer-term consequences and feedback mechanisms associated with ocean acidification is to study similar periods in Earth's past. This project focuses on Ocean Anoxic Event 2 (OAE2), a 94-million-year-old event that involved global depletion of marine oxygen (anoxia) that was caused by high levels of volcanism. Volcanic carbon dioxide emissions at this time may have also led to widespread ocean acidification, in a manner similar to modern ocean acidification. This project seeks to evaluate the spatial and temporal relationship between volcanism and acidification at two sites during OAE2 using geochemical analysis of isotope ratios preserved in the corresponding rocks. Rock samples were crushed, dissolved, and analyzed for isotopic ratios via thermal ionization and isotope ratio mass spectrometric techniques. Ongoing calcium, carbon, and osmium isotopic analysis of samples from these two sites may suggest a complex interplay between volcanism, acidification, and post-depositional chemical alteration before, during, and after OAE2. These results could enhance scientific understanding of the spatial variability of acidification during OAE2, and assist in projections of future, human-driven acidification impacts.

title: Early Adversity, Meaning-Making, and the Construction of Narrative Identity among Exceptionally Generative Latina Leaders
abstract: How do individuals sustain moral commitment amid enduring hardship? This study examines how highly generative Latina activists interpret adversity and construct narratives that sustain their work in advocacy and community organizing. Focusing on lives shaped by chronic insecurity, gendered violence, and political instability, it asks what narrative forms enable sustained commitment to others. Using an idiographic qualitative design, the study analyzes autobiographical interviews with ten Latina activists engaged in advocacy related to forced disappearance, child abuse, Indigenous political participation, and gender-based violence. Interviews were transcribed, translated, and analyzed inductively for narrative identity processes. Across cases, participants structured their narratives by foregrounding early disadvantage alongside moments of opportunity, followed by a turning point: the recognition that their suffering was shared. From this, commitment to others took shape as a responsibility they could not refuse. Suffering is not left in the past; it remains an ongoing point of connection to others' pain. Participants stay closely connected to their sources of grief and interpret both victims and perpetrators through relational and contextual understandings. Action and suffering unfold together: the same conditions that threaten participants also sustain their work by giving it meaning. What participants describe as healing is not resolution, but the ability to continue while remaining connected to pain, which enables them to support others. This study introduces collective redemption to describe this narrative form. In contrast to dominant U.S. models of redemption, these findings suggest that generativity emerges through sustained engagement with hardship rather than from its resolution.

title: Language Deprivation from Structural Violence: Trauma, LDS, and Implications
abstract: While existing literature documents both the harms of language deprivation and high rates of trauma among deaf individuals, few studies explicitly connect these phenomena. This paper questions whether psychological harm and trauma in deaf populations can be primarily attributable to language deprivation rather than the condition of being deaf. It also examines the proposal of Language Deprivation Syndrome (LDS) and its implications for how these outcomes are classified in mental health contexts. This project uses a qualitative synthesis of historical accounts, policy analysis, and peer-reviewed research to examine how educational systems, healthcare practices, and language access shape early development in deaf children. The scope includes scholarship on deaf education, mental health outcomes, and emerging theoretical frameworks. Across studies, language deprivation is consistently associated with cognitive delays, reduced educational attainment, and higher rates of depression, anxiety, and trauma exposure. Findings indicate that language deprivation is primarily a structural issue shaped by educational policy, limited access to sign language, and societal attitudes toward deafness. Evidence further suggests that psychological harm in deaf populations is better explained by this structural deprivation than by deafness itself. While emerging research on LDS identifies a pattern of developmental outcomes linked to deprivation, it also raises concerns about the pathologization of socially produced harm. Recognizing language deprivation as a preventable trauma reframes it as a public health and human rights issue. These findings underscore the need for early bilingual language access and systemic reforms in education, healthcare, and family support to improve outcomes and reduce harm.

title: Gender-Based Personality Differences in Early-Stage Entrepreneurs
abstract: This study provides a comparison of early-stage entrepreneurs and successful entrepreneurs, while investigating gender-based personality differences within early-stage entrepreneurs. Utilizing a battery of assessments, this research identifies that while early-stage entrepreneurs share a foundational profile with successful founders, distinct differences exist in key areas such as ambition, learning approach, and prudence. Successful entrepreneurs demonstrated higher achievement orientation and lower prudence, suggesting that flexibility and risk-tolerance are critical drivers of success. Early-stage entrepreneurs most deviated from successful entrepreneurs in their derailers. Higher relative scores in cautiousness, diligence, and dutifulness likely impede the early-stage entrepreneur's ability to make rapid decisions. Conversely, successful entrepreneurs scored higher on the mischievous and imaginative scales, reflecting a greater propensity for limit-testing and unconventional methodology. Gender analysis revealed significant differences in negative emotionality (neuroticism) as well as in cognitive and affective empathy, with women in both, which is also consistent with broader population trends. However, women's higher scores in empathy did not diminish their self-perceived leadership capacity or social potency, which remained equal across genders. Going against trends in the broader population, there was no significant difference in scores related to achievement motivation or competitiveness. In the general population, men tend to score higher, but the competitiveness that characterizes entrepreneurs could explain why we fail to see that trend between genders in the early-stage entrepreneurs. Overall, these findings suggest that while "successful" leadership traits are relatively gender-neutral, internal affective processing styles and factors such as developmental stage (age) play significant roles in the entrepreneurial trajectory.

title: Neural Correlates of Spectral and Temporal Perceptual Strategies in Music-in-Noise Performance
abstract: Listening-in-noise requires listeners to extract precise auditory cues from a mixture of target sound streams and background noise. While music-in-noise perception has garnered recent interest as an assessment of auditory processing beyond speech, the neural mechanisms underlying individual differences in performance remain unclear. In particular, it is unknown whether variability in music-in-noise perception reflects distinct perceptual strategies that map onto neural encoding differences. This study aims to identify neural correlates of performance on the Music-in-Noise Test (MINT) by examining how music-in-noise perception is supported by different perceptual cues, and how these strategies relate to measures of auditory processing. Young adults aged 18-25 without extensive music experience (N = 20) completed the Music in Noise Test (MINT), which isolates performance based on pitch, rhythm, spatial, visual, and predictive cues. Principal component analysis of MINT subtests identified a single dominant component, separating pitch-based from more rhythm and visual performance strategies. Neural responses to music presented in quiet and noise were recorded using the Frequency-Following Response (FFR) and encoding strength at the fundamental frequency and harmonics was examined as a function of the behavioral strategy. Listeners with pitch-driven MINT performance exhibited stronger neural encoding of the fundamental frequency and harmonics in noise compared to those relying on non-spectral cues. These results demonstrate that behavioral strategies for music perception in noise are directly reflected in neural encoding of acoustic cues.

title: The Role of Serine Palmitolyltransferase Single Small Unit B in the Skin Barrier
abstract: When skin barrier function is compromised, skin diseases, such as eczema (atopic dermatitis, AD), can develop. AD, characterized by dry, itchy, and inflamed skin, reduces the quality of life for many individuals. The cause of AD is still not fully understood, and more effective, long-term treatments are needed. Ceramides are natural fats important to the skin barrier, assisting in moisture retention and protection. People with AD often have lower ceramide levels. After analyzing skin samples from AD patients and healthy individuals, we found that those with severe eczema were associated with having shorter ceramide lengths. Longer ceramides are thought to help form stronger skin barriers, while shorter ones may weaken them. A protein complex called SPT helps determine ceramide length early in the production process. One component of the complex, SPTSSB, is important for producing longer ceramides in the skin. Previous data suggest that SPTSSB levels are lower in human skin with AD. Investigating the effects of SPTSSB expression could reveal SPT’s role in AD development, providing insight into potential directions for AD treatment. This study employed three-dimensional lab grown skin to model human skin development. The amount of SPTSSB was lowered and the changes were observed. To study these changes, we used laboratory techniques that measure gene activity and visualize the skin in culture. Reducing SPTSSB resulted in lower levels of key skin development markers, indicating impaired skin development. The study findings suggest that SPTSSB is important for skin barrier function, making it a potential treatment target for eczema.

title: Beyond the Cytoskeleton: Vimentin as a Regulator of Chemotherapy Resistance in Glioblastoma
abstract: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor with a median survival of 15 months, in part due to the tumor's adaptive resistance to temozolomide (TMZ), the first-line chemotherapeutic agent in GBM treatment. However, strategies to overcome resistance and improve patient outcomes remain elusive. Recent research suggests that VIM, a cytoskeletal protein overexpressed in GBM and a validated marker of invasion and poor prognosis, can also function as a DNA-binding protein in the nucleus, indicating potential roles in gene regulation. This study investigates whether VIM contributes to TMZ resistance through its nuclear-associated functions. To evaluate the role of VIM in TMZ resistance, we utilized multiple patient-derived xenograft (PDX) GBM cell lines treated with TMZ. Changes in VIM expression and subcellular localization were assessed using Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. To map VIM-DNA interactions, we performed CUT&RUN (Cleavage Under Targets & Release Using Nuclease) followed by downstream bioinformatics analyses to identify VIM-bound gene regions and associated pathways. We found that both cytoplasmic and nuclear VIM expression is increased by TMZ treatment. CUT&RUN analysis further revealed that VIM binds to regulatory regions of genes associated with TMZ resistance programs at 72 hours post-TMZ exposure. These findings suggest that VIM may act as a regulator of gene expression contributing to chemoresistance in GBM through means beyond its conventional cytoskeletal roles. Collectively, this work highlights a previously underexplored role of VIM in GBM biology and supports its potential as a therapeutic target for overcoming TMZ resistance.

title: Interrupted! Using a Virtual Museum Video Game to Study Task-Switching
abstract: Empirical task switching studies investigating the ability to flexibly redirect attention, often rely on strict parameters to maintain a controlled environment. However, this does not capture naturalistic conditions involving exploration and everyday distractors. Gallery Glimpse was developed to address this, a video game evaluating naturalistic working- and episodic-memory suitable for stationary research participants, i.e. intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG). Participants alternate between viewing art pieces in a museum (episodic memory encoding) and interpolating memorization of phone numbers (working memory distractor). This study establishes normative behavioral data on cognitive flexibility in a control cohort aged 6–57 (n=89). We hypothesized controls would exhibit a transient “switch cost,”—decreased episodic memory accuracy immediately following the working memory distractor—while the iEEG cohort would demonstrate impaired cognitive flexibility via a prolonged switch cost. A mixed-effects model confirmed a switch cost in controls. The distractor task disrupted memory performance on the first art piece with improved memory accuracy on subsequent art pieces (β = 0.07, z = 6.54, p < .001). The model also identified a significant practice effect, with improved accuracy in the second to last (β = 0.05, z = 4.43, p < .001) and last (β = 0.07, z = 5.82, p < .001) rooms. iEEG cohort analyses will identify behavioral differences during the same period. This work will establish the use of Gallery Glimpse for bridging the gap between controlled experimental settings and real-world cognitive flexibility, while also providing a framework for understanding epilepsy-related memory impairments.

title: Group Singing as Treatment for Children's Wellness
abstract: Out of the Covid-19 pandemic emerged a mental health crisis, resulting from the prolonged periods of isolation and online interaction. This crisis was especially prevalent amongst children and adolescents, as younger people reported higher levels of depression and anxiety. In response to this crisis, Dr. Sarah Bartolome created the Music for Childhood Well-being Initiative (MCWI), an initiative exploring the impact of singing in a group on children's mental health and wellbeing. In this initiative, 8-week long sessions were conducted where a group of children aged 8-12 were led by an instructor to sing and engage in breathing and stretching exercises. As an Emerging Scholar research assistant, my involvement in this initiative included setting up surveys for the participants to complete, helping participants put on the heart-rate monitoring device we used to collect their heart rate and heart rate variability data, accompanying the singing by playing the piano during sessions, and administering closing interviews for each session. As the sessions progressed, I observed how these sessions led the participants to bond over a sense of community. This became something that all the participants looked forward to every week, and even if participants admitted to entering the room feeling tired, they usually left feeling happy after the session's activities. Further implications of this research could involve the exploration of utilizing group singing as a potential mental health treatment for demographics beyond children, as it has proved to be effective amongst children in MCWI sessions.

title: Living, Working, and Playing: Asian American Environmental Justice Before the Movement
abstract: In 1991, over one thousand environmental activists of color gathered in Washington, D.C. for the First National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit, marking the beginning of the environmental justice (EJ) movement. To formally define EJ, they ratified the seventeen Principles of Environmental Justice, highlighting the unequal environmental burdens that low-income communities of color face and redefining the environment itself to include not only the natural wilderness, but also spaces where humans live, work, and play. Despite the movement's increased inclusivity and reach since 1991, scholars and the general public have overlooked Asian American EJ activism because of the pervasive model minority myth, which casts Asians as deferential, apolitical machines alienated from nature. To counter this misconception, my paper examines three cases of Asian American organizing that contain EJ characteristics but lack scholarly analysis of this dimension because they occurred prior to the movement. Using the seventeen Principles, I analyze San Francisco Chinatown's bubonic plague outbreak in 1900, Hawai'i's sugar strike in 1946, and San Francisco Manilatown's International Hotel movement in the 1970s. I argue that, throughout their long history of organizing around issues like civil rights, labor rights, and housing, Asian Americans were fighting for environmental justice long before the movement began. My paper demonstrates it is possible to apply the modern EJ framework to pre-movement history, and I encourage historians to reexamine their areas of study accordingly. Ultimately, I aim to dispel stereotypes about Asian American apoliticalness and uncover a hidden thread of Asian American history.

title: Isolating the Utility of Planning Against a Dynamic Threat in Naturalistic Decision-Making
abstract: Traditionally, research on choice-based behavior has relied on simple, static experimental setups that lack ecological validity. To address this limitation, the Dombeck Lab and MacIver Lab have developed a large arena with reconfigurable obstacles and an autonomous robotic predator, allowing for the systematic manipulation of environmental structure and threat dynamics. Using high-resolution tracking of a mouse's position and velocity, this system enables detailed characterization of navigational strategies, escape behaviors, and decision-making processes during predator evasion and reward-seeking. Previous work using this arena demonstrated that increasing environmental complexity through the addition of obstacles enhances the utility of planning; while in open, obstacle-free environments, mice tend to rely on habitual, stereotyped routes that minimize deliberation. In the present study, we ask whether planning-like behavior can emerge even in a low-complexity, open arena when a dynamic and behaviorally relevant element is introduced. Specifically, we examine whether the presence of a behaviorally-complex, mobile, interactive threat is sufficient to disrupt habitual navigation and elicit behavioral signatures consistent with planning. By isolating dynamic threat from static spatial complexity, this work aims to clarify the conditions under which planning becomes computationally advantageous in naturalistic decision-making.

title: Exploring fathers' health behavior motivations to leverage healthcare engagement in the perinatal period: A qualitative study
abstract: Commonly, fathers engage in their partner's healthcare in the perinatal (e.g. obstetrics appointments) but underutilize their own healthcare and preventive care services. Thus, researching ways to better engage fathers with healthcare services by leveraging perinatal contact and fathers' perinatal-specific motivations may provide opportunities for health promotion of fathers. Thus, semi-structured interviews with new fathers (n=30) and paired mothers (n=10) in Prentice Women's Hospital were conducted to explore perspectives on and experiences of fathers' health behaviors in the perinatal period. Interview transcripts were cleaned and thematically analyzed based on the Health Belief Model. It was found that fathers were generally highly motivated to maintain or improve their own health in the perinatal period. Being an "active father," longevity for family's sake, and "groundedness" from new fatherhood were important motivations for engaging in positive health behaviors (i.e. exercise, healthy diet, limiting substances use). Low perceived susceptibility to chronic disease and social norms against healthcare engagement were cited as deterrents for preventive healthcare utilization. Time constraints, insurance, and difficulty navigating the healthcare system were cited as barriers to actionable healthcare engagement despite increased motivation. Both fathers and mothers mentioned that leveraging family-centered rather than individual motivations while providing ease to healthcare access (e.g. health screenings in OB settings; efficient primary care referrals) could be effective. This study highlights the potential efficacy of the perinatal period as a leveraging period for engaging fathers with healthcare and offers insight into more broadly expanding health programming for fathers.

title: Effects of Independence and Interdependence Priming on Big Five Personality Trait Reporting
abstract: Personality assessments such as the Big Five are often assumed to reflect stable individual traits, yet growing evidence suggests that responses may be shaped by contextual and cultural factors, including how individuals construe themselves in relation to others. This study examined whether priming independence versus interdependence influences personality trait reporting, and whether individual differences in self-construal predict variation in responses. Participants (N = 117) first completed baseline Big Five (BFI-2) and self-construal measures. In a second session, participants were randomly assigned to an independence or interdependence priming task before completing anchoring vignettes designed to reduce reference group bias in personality judgments. The priming manipulation did not produce significant group-level differences in vignette-adjusted personality ratings. As a result, multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine whether individual differences in self-construal predicted trait reporting while controlling for baseline personality. Across all five traits, baseline Big Five scores were strong and consistent predictors of vignette-adjusted ratings (all p & .001). However, neither interdependence nor independence scores significantly predicted trait ratings for any domain (all p > .13). These findings suggest that personality reporting, even when adjusted for reference group bias, is largely stable and not easily influenced by brief contextual primes or individual differences in self-construal. This has implications for theories of cultural variation in personality, highlighting potential limits on the malleability of self-reported traits in experimental contexts.

title: Fingertip-Sized Wireless Button Sensors for Health Monitoring in Neonatal and Pediatric Patients
abstract: The button sensors project aims to develop fingertip-sized devices for wirelessly monitoring vital signs of preterm patients in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). Three discrete units-ECG/EEG (chest/head), PPG (head), and mechano-acoustic (peripheral)-work in tandem to provide comprehensive measurements of key vitals: heart rate, respiration, blood oxygen level, EEG, heart rate variability, sleep, motion, and temperature. Each unit includes electronic components encapsulated by medical-grade silicone or epoxy, which protects sensitive neonatal skin from abrasion and ensures longevity of the device. One significant technical achievement of the project was successfully miniaturizing photoplethysmography (PPG) for the head unit, enabling measurement of peripheral oxygen saturation with increased space optimization and power-efficiency. The sensors are supported by two power supply options-wireless power transfer technology or a miniature magnet-connected battery-which can be easily interchanged to reduce data dropouts. Data streams continuously and wirelessly to a smartphone app and uploads to the cloud, which allows clinicians to monitor changes in real time. By implementing wireless communication, this design overcomes the limitations of conventional wired systems with rigid interfaces, protecting neonates from further skin injuries and vascular complications. Ultimately, by offering a fully wireless, ultra-miniaturized device and an intuitive real-time monitoring platform, this integrated system represents a significant advancement in enabling parent kangaroo care, streamlining clinical workflows, allowing unobstructed movement, and delivering accurate, minimally intrusive monitoring in even the most sensitive patients.

title: Altered Foodways: The Impact of Colonialism on PCOS Prevalence in the Andes
abstract: Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) is a reproductive and metabolic disorder caused by both genetic and dietary factors. The prevalence of PCOS within a population is particularly high among the indigenous populations of the global south, compared to rates in European populations. This study examines the prevalence of PCOS among indigenous and mestizo Andean populations and considers the impact of colonialism and changing foodways on the emergence of this condition. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic literature review compiled academic journal articles on PCOS rates, foodways, and Spanish colonial policy in the indigenous Andes from the 16th century to 20th century. The implementation of a tribute economy and debt peonage system disrupted indigenous agricultural practices and access to domestic foods, resulting in changes in dietary patterns. Additionally, increase in trade from lowlands to highlands resulted in increased availability of non-traditional foodstuffs, creating social pressure to adopt a non-traditional diet for social mobility. Both of these developments resulted in increased reliance on imported and processed foods over traditional, domestic foods that continued into the 20th century. Comparative evidence suggests that shifting from a subsistence diet to one high in simple carbohydrates and fats resulted in body composition and metabolic health that promoted the emergence of PCOS. Understanding the effect of colonialism on contemporary agrarian practices and foodways unveils underlying systems that raise PCOS prevalence within this population, allowing them to be targeted for treatment.

title: Internal Fact-Checking and the Crisis of Trust in News Mediaa
abstract: This thesis examines the role of fact-checking in addressing the crisis of trust in American news media, asking whether current practices meaningfully improve public understanding or credibility. While fact-checking has become a prominent journalistic tool, this project argues that its dominant form-external, post-publication verification of political claims-faces structural limitations that prevent it from achieving its intended audience-facing goals. Drawing on interviews with leading practitioners, including Glenn Kessler of The Washington Post, Kimberly Ammiano of the CBS Evening News research team, and Zach Helfand of The New Yorker, as well as historical and case analysis and research in media psychology, the thesis compares external fact-checking with internal, pre-publication verification processes. It finds a disconnect between the "imagined" effects of external fact-checking, as described by journalists, and its "real" effects on audiences, which are shaped by factors such as selective exposure, motivated reasoning, and declining institutional trust. While fact-checking has at times imposed reputational costs on political actors, evidence suggests it rarely produces lasting changes in public beliefs. The project argues that strengthening internal fact-checking within original reporting-rather than relying primarily on reactive, standalone corrections-offers a more effective way to ensure accuracy reaches audiences at the point of consumption. By reframing fact-checking as a proactive rather than corrective practice, this research offers a potential solution in the consolidation of fact-checking efforts that prioritizes internal fact-checking, and contributes to ongoing debates about journalistic responsibility, media credibility, and the future of truth-seeking in a fragmented information environment.

title: Using arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) as indicators of belowground responses to urban river corridor restoration in Chicago
abstract: Urban prairie restorations are increasingly used to recover ecosystem health and services in river corridors. However, belowground responses to restoration, particularly by soil arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF), are not well characterized in these systems. AMF form symbiotic relationships with plant roots, enhancing nutrient and water uptake, particularly nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), in exchange for carbon (C). Their external hyphal networks contribute to nutrient cycling, soil aggregation, and improved soil structure, supporting plant establishment in restored ecosystems. Because of these functions, AMF abundance can serve as a useful benchmark for evaluating restoration progress. In this study, we investigated the relationship between AMF hyphal abundance, soil properties and restoration status in three sites that comprised a restoration gradient along the Chicago River corridor (unrestored control; early and late-stage restoration). While this gradient allows for initial comparisons, the limited number of sites constrains broader generalization. Results to date suggest that differences in soil properties across sites, rather than distance from the river, are the primary drivers of variation along the restoration gradient. Notably, the late-stage restoration site showed lower C and higher P levels relative to unrestored and early-restoration sites. Consistent with our expectations, AMF abundance was highest in the restored site and lowest in the unrestored site. This pattern aligns with lower nutrient availability in restored soils, where plants increasingly rely on AMF to support nutrient acquisition. These results highlight the importance of belowground recovery during restoration and reinforce the value of incorporating AMF abundance into monitoring frameworks to better assess ecosystem recovery and guide future restoration practices.

title: Altered Kinetics and Voltage Dependence of Activation in a Pathogenic KCNH1 Potassium Channel Variant
abstract: Genetic variants in neuronal potassium channel genes are associated with epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders. Variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel KV10.1, cause two closely related neurodevelopmental disorders: Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS) and Zimmermann-Laband Syndrome (ZLS). These disorders affect young children with epilepsy, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and other non-neuronal features. Despite this clinical association, the mechanisms by which disease-causing variants alter channel function remain poorly understood. We investigated the functional effects of R357Q, the most recurrent pathogenic KCNH1 variant. Human embryonic kidney (HEK293) cells were transiently transfected with R357Q or wild-type KCNH1 plasmid, and potassium currents were measured using whole-cell voltage clamp electrophysiology. This technique allows precise control of membrane potential while recording ion channel activity. Cells expressing the R357Q variant exhibited markedly faster channel opening (activation kinetics) and altered dependence on voltage. We also investigated the hypothesis that strong pre-pulse hyperpolarization preceding channel activation slows kinetics in R357Q. We examined this effect using two alternatively spliced KCNH1 isoforms (isoform 1, isoform 2). Hyperpolarized pre-pulses significantly slowed activation of the R357Q variant in both channel isoforms and produced different kinetics across both wildtype isoforms. Notably, isoform 2 contains a short deletion in the extracellular S3-S4 linker region, suggesting that this region may influence gating properties. These findings suggest that altered voltage sensitivity and gating behavior contribute to channel dysfunction in TBS and ZLS. Understanding how specific mutations disrupt potassium channel function provides mechanistic insight into epilepsy pathogenesis and may inform future therapeutic strategies targeting channel gating dynamics.

title: Structural and Functional Insights into ProU Regulation: Investigating CBS-Mediated Inhibition in Yersinia pestis
abstract: Pathogens often encounter sudden environmental changes as they move between hosts. Changes in salt concentrations can cause osmotic shock, leading to a rapid influx or efflux of water from the pathogen to balance the difference in salt, killing it. Bacteria can protect themselves against osmotic shock by importing osmoprotectant molecules, often by utilizing ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters. These transporters hydrolyze ATP to move substrates against a gradient into or out of the cell. My project focuses on the osmoprotectant ABC importer ProU found in the pathogen Yersinia pestis, the causative agent of the Black Plague. The ProU importer imports the osmoprotectant molecule glycine betaine to stabilize intracellular salt and charge concentrations, thereby preventing water loss from the bacterium. ProU is believed to be regulated by the cystathionine-v-synthase (CBS) regulatory domain, based on research on the related transporter OpuA. The CBS domain in OpuA inhibits transporter function upon binding cyclic-di-AMP, a known stress response molecule and secondary messenger. To uncover the regulatory mechanism of the ProU transporter, the ProU CBS domain was separated from ProU and crystallized. Two apo structures of the ProU CBS domain were determined by X-ray crystallography, revealing a dramatically different orientation compared to the CBS domain of OpuA when binding cyclic-di-AMP. The CBS structure can help provide vital information on how ProU is regulated and offer a more targeted approach to treating pathogens amid increased pathogen antibiotic resistance, as many pathogens rely on osmoprotectant transporters for their infectivity.

title: Psychological States and Responses to Constructive Friendship Criticism: Comparing Self-Affirmation, Felt Security, and Ego-Threat
abstract: Constructive criticism (CC) can promote behavioral improvement and strengthen relationships, yet recipients often respond defensively to evaluative feedback. Prior research suggests that psychological states such as self-affirmation, felt security, and ego-threat impact openness to criticism, particularly in threatening evaluative contexts. However, it remains unclear whether these same states shape responses to constructive criticism, which combines negative evaluation with benevolent intent. The present study examined whether momentary psychological states that buffer against or induce threat influence responses to constructive criticism within friendships. Participants (N = 204) were randomly assigned to a self-affirmation, felt-security, ego-threat, or control condition before reading two standardized scenarios depicting constructive criticism from a close friend. Participants then completed measures assessing perceived hostility, trust in the feedback and feedback-giver, receptiveness to feedback, and adaptive and maladaptive relational responses. Contrary to predictions, the experimental conditions did not differ significantly across any outcome variables. Across conditions, participants generally perceived the criticism as highly non-hostile and responded with high levels of trust, receptiveness, and adaptive responding. Perceiving the criticism as non-hostile was associated with greater trust in the feedback, which in turn was associated with greater receptiveness and more adaptive relational responding. These findings suggest that when criticism is delivered constructively, the framing and perceived intent of the feedback may play a more important role in shaping responses than recipients’ temporary psychological states. More broadly, the results raise the possibility that constructive criticism may not evoke sufficient threat for transient self-threat and threat-buffering states to substantially influence evaluative processing.

title: Poetic Medicine: Black Feminist Poetics of Cancer and HIV/AIDS
abstract: Public health research indicates disparities in health outcomes along racialized and gendered lines. This includes health inequities for Black femmes who are faced with oppression by virtue of both race and gender. The subjective experiences of Black femmes are lost to the privileging of biomedical knowledge and a reliance on medical systems built on the exploitation of Black bodies. This project analyzes Black women's poetry and creative nonfiction writing about health and wellbeing to examine the experiences of illness not legible to medical systems, drawing comparisons between cancer and HIV/AIDS. I argue that poetry is a tool of personal and collective healing, a space of worldbuilding and an opportunity to illuminate and make communal internal experiences of precarity, and oppression that stem from the individual and individuating experience of illness. Yet, all illnesses are not the same, and so I highlight differences between poetry about cancer and HIV/AIDS. The poetics of cancer often originates from a confrontation with the self through the body, while poetry about HIV/AIDS confronts self-definition and social meaning. Working towards an interrogation of the relationships between normativity, medical systems, and understandings of the self, "Poetic Medicine" shows that personal writing is a tool of self and communal study. Throughout, I elucidate aspects of wellbeing that medical systems fail to palliate (and that they often instead harm), especially for Black femme patients living with disease. Ultimately, I hope to broaden public health practice by infusing scientific and medical processes with the suff of poetry.

title: Investigating the Effect of Linguistic Labeling on Object Categorization and Memory in 7 and 12-Month-Olds: Evidence from a "Peek-a-Boo" Occlusion Task
abstract: Current research suggests that infants can develop language categories as early as six months of age through verbal communication in their environments. However, it is unclear how language labels affect an infant's memory of object categories in more dynamic situations. It is also unknown how persistent language categories are with aging, especially in the newborn-infant stage of development. Therefore, two studies in 12-month and 7-month olds were conducted to investigate if naming objects with distinct language labels with a change-detection task positively impacted their object categorization skills. Stuffed animals were shown with verbal pseudowords (e.g. boff or dax) in the learning phase. In two test trials, a stuffed animal from the learning phase was shown and then covered with a blocker. After removing the blocker, the stuffed animal was either the same as before the blocker was placed or different. The infants' level of surprise, and therefore individuation of the animal as an object category, was determined from their average looking time after the blocker was removed. As predicted, there was a significant increase in average looking time in the distinct naming Within Change condition in 12-month-olds. This indicates that strong object individuation occurred, and that it persisted over the occlusion task. Preliminary findings show that more participants are needed to show statistical significance in the 7-month-old study. We believe that linguistically naming objects can improve an infant's object categorization and memory skills, which may influence how caregivers interact with children to improve their language and cognitive development.

title: Development of a Fluorescence-Based Endomicroscope System for Quantitative Assessment of Pediatric Aspiration
abstract: Aspiration, the accidental inhalation of foreign material into the lungs, is a severe, yet critically understudied, clinical danger for pediatric and neurologically impaired patients that can lead to life-threatening respiratory complications. Current diagnostic methods, such as videofluoroscopic swallow studies, only provide indirect, qualitative assessments. They lack the sensitivity to directly visualize or measure aspirated material at the microscopic level. To address this gap, we present a proof-of-concept fluorescence endomicroscope designed to directly detect and quantify aspirated fluorescent particles (microspheres) within lung tissue. Our system utilizes a specialized optical setup, featuring a broadband LED, wavelength filters, and a high-resolution sensor, to illuminate the tissue and capture the fluorescence of these microscopic particles, acting as a proxy for aspiration severity. We successfully demonstrated that this system reliably visualizes microspheres in lung tissue samples. By applying an image analysis algorithm, we quantified particle density, providing an objective metric of the aspiration burden. Experimental results showed that while thicker, physiologically relevant tissue reduced image contrast due to light scattering, the particles remained clearly identifiable. System resolution easily distinguished individual 10-micrometer particles, and sampling analysis confirmed that this performance is limited by optical physics rather than sensor constraints. These findings establish fluorescence endomicroscopy as a viable method for directly visualizing and measuring microscale aspiration. This platform introduces a vital shift from subjective observation to precise, quantitative measurement, offering a powerful new framework for early diagnosis, severity grading, targeted treatment monitoring in highly vulnerable patient populations, and general aspiration study.

title: How Bacteria Tell Time: Mathematical Models of the Cyanobacterial Circadian Clock
abstract: The cyanobacterial circadian clock is a biochemical process that enables cyanobacteria to predict changes in their environment. Timekeeping of the cyanobacterial clock is accomplished through routine, ATP-dependent cycling between the phosphorylation states of the clock protein KaiC and its binding with mediator proteins KaiA and KaiB. The cyanobacterial clock has been traditionally modeled using ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that produce predictable and periodic trajectories of protein concentration over time. In nature, however, this biochemical process is subject to biological noise, including random fluctuations in environmental conditions, rate constants, and protein concentrations. This project develops "noisy" stochastic models of the cyanobacterial clock to test the validity of the ODE framework under biologically relevant noise conditions and to better analyze sensitivities of this biochemical process. The noise tolerance of each parameter was determined by identifying statistical variation between the trajectory of stochastic simulations and the period of the ODE model. Statistical analysis of the stochastic simulations revealed that the model is highly tolerant to random fluctuation in ATP and the concentration of unphosphorylated KaiC, consistent with the fact that these parameters are most susceptible to noise in a natural environment. Analysis also revealed that the model is sensitive to minor fluctuation in the concentrations of KaiA and sequestered KaiC, a new insight gained through stochastic modeling. These results exhibit how stochastic modeling can validate and refine mathematical models of biochemical processes and reveal underlying sensitivities of a biochemical system to drive future experimentation.

title: High-Throughput Discovery of Trispecific Antibodies for Cancer Therapies Using MegaMolecules.
abstract: Immunotherapy is transforming oncology by leveraging antibodies to target specific cancer cell surface receptors, thereby reducing the off-target side effects associated with nonspecific treatments like chemotherapy. Once bound, these antibodies eliminate tumors by blocking growth signals, recruiting immune cells, or delivering toxic payloads. Multispecific antibodies—which bind to multiple receptors simultaneously—offer even greater potential by disrupting several signaling pathways at once, increasing binding strength through enhanced avidity, and increasing selectivity for cancer cells. Modern drug discovery is built on high-throughput screening of large and structurally diverse libraries of candidates to identify those with activity and narrow down millions of possibilities to a few promising leads. However, synthesis of large libraries of trispecific antibodies is a significant challenge. MegaMolecules provide a modular platform that enables rapid, precise assembly of multispecific antibodies. Rather than designing whole, rigid IgG scaffolds, megamolecules utilize high-affinity, covalent enzyme-inhibitor reactions to prepare multivalent antibodies with unprecedented scale and stability. In this project, we utilized the megamolecule architecture to construct a diverse library of 300 trispecific antibodies targeting numerous commonly expressed breast cancer epitopes from a base library of 23 fusion proteins. By successfully synthesizing and characterizing this library, this project demonstrates the unique efficacy of the megamolecule platform to address the prevailing limitations of immunotherapeutic design, establishing a scalable foundation for the discovery of the next generation of multispecific cancer therapies.

title: Clean Conscience: Exploring College Students' Enactment of Environmental Beliefs Through Domestic Labor
abstract: In the face of climate change and the imminent threat it poses to global human welfare, what explains disparities in individuals' level of concern about environmental issues and subsequent willingness to act on this concern? The feminization of environmental action has been well-documented since the start of the 20th century and is particularly evident in studies of middle-aged adults' household labor dynamics. However, this extensive literature largely overlooks college students, who constitute a population of interest as the next generation of environmental decision-makers. Through semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 21 students at Northwestern University, I endeavored to answer the question of how gender influences the development and enactment of college students' environmental beliefs. I tested three hypotheses regarding feminized environmental action from the aforementioned literature: the maternal responsibility, knowledge support, and economic salience hypotheses. The distinctive characteristics of private, four-year colleges like Northwestern challenge the norms inherent to each hypothesis; such institutions are a site where students live independently and create less-formalized relationships, gain knowledge and analytical skills regardless of their gender, and are encouraged to cultivate an economic mindset. My findings indicate that, despite this unique context, gender socialization remains strongly influential to students' environmental beliefs and behaviors, as evidenced by participants' tendency to align themselves with mainstream gender expectations through their actions as well as the language they used when justifying them. This indicates that shifting norms (gendered and otherwise) could potentially bring about widespread behavioral change-an implication warranting further research and attention from sociologists and policymakers alike.

title: Probabilistic Neural Operator for Dynamical Systems Under Uncertainty
abstract: In everyday life, we encounter many systems that evolve over time, known as dynamical systems. Examples include vibrations in structures, weather patterns, financial markets, and the spread of diseases. Scientists and engineers have studied these systems for many years, but traditional models often struggle to take full advantage of the large amounts of data now available. Such models also rarely tell us how reliable their predictions are. Our research aims to develop a new data-driven modeling approach using neural operators, a modern machine learning technique that learns how entire systems change over time. Unlike standard models, our approach not only predicts future behavior based on past observations but also estimates how confident those predictions are. To achieve this, we incorporate ideas from statistics, such as quantile regression and Bayesian methods, to explicitly account for uncertainty. By doing so, the model can capture both errors in the data (from sensors that record noisy, imperfect measurements) and limitations in the model itself. As a result, our method produces predictions along with confidence intervals, giving users a clearer understanding of possible outcomes and risks. We compare our approach with existing methods that estimate uncertainty. Preliminary results suggest that our approach achieves similar or better predictive performance, while providing more trustworthy confidence intervals with a simpler and more efficient framework. Such reliability is especially important for decision-making in areas like healthcare, climate science, and finance, where uncertainty plays a critical role.

title: Knockdown of Clock in Ventral Tegmental Area Dopamine Neurons Influences Bipolar-Like Behaviors and Sleep Deprivation Responses in Mice
abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) affects approximately 1 in 150 adults worldwide and is a leading cause of disability, typically emerging in adolescence. BD is characterized by dramatic shifts between manic and depressive mood states, linked to increased and decreased activity of dopamine (DA) neurons, respectively. Sleep and circadian rhythm disruption are also strongly associated with mood cycling and BD. The circadian transcription factor Clock has been implicated in BD by GWAS and modulates DA function in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), a major hub of reward-related DA signaling. Previous work shows that Clock disruption in mice can produce mania-like phenotypes and alter depression-related behavior. However, effects of knocking down Clock in VTA DA neurons are poorly understood, even less so when coupled with acute sleep deprivation. Notably, existing studies with Clock manipulations offer contradictory results: global knockdown (KD) resulted in an increased mania-like phenotype characterized by reduced depression-like behavior, but VTA-specific knockdown led to increased depression-like behavior. In preliminary behavioral testing, neonatal VTA Clock KD mice showed reduced anxiety-like behavior relative to controls, consistent with an increased mania-like phenotype. After sleep deprivation, KD mice also exhibited lower anxiety levels than controls. At baseline, KD mice displayed more depression-like behaviors. Together, these results suggest that early postnatal reduction of Clock in VTA DA neurons can simultaneously reduce anxiety- and increase depression-related behaviors, and modulate behavioral responses to sleep deprivation. Manipulating Clock and sleep at different points in development may help elucidate developmental mechanisms linking circadian dysregulation and DA circuitry to BD.

title: The King and Queen of Rock: Little Richard, Religion, and the Stipulations of Black Queer Fame
abstract: Little Richard, born Richard Wayne Penniman in 1932, is widely recognized as a key founder of rock and roll. However, the intersections of his Blackness, queerness, and religiosity have received limited attention from scholars. This paper examines why Penniman continually oscillated between embracing and rejecting his queerness across his seventy-year career, arguing that his global stardom amplified criticism from Black and white populations, exacerbating his lifelong struggle with sexuality and faith. Using his 1984 authorized biography, magazine profiles, and television interviews, along with modern-day scholarship on Black queerness, race theory, and music history, the paper traces Penniman's public positions on his queerness from the 1950s until his passing in 2020. Each withdrawal into intensified religiosity is a clear response from Penniman to external pressures. Such stresses included his father's violent rejection, the AIDS epidemic, and declining health near the end of his life. When he returned to openness, it was a display of irrepressible queerness, with the stage as the place where fashion and extravagance could become a language for his identity. The research concludes that Penniman's life is not a narrative of contradictions but rather of the consequences of Black queer people being stuck in the interlocking oppressive systems of white supremacy, homophobia, and the institution of religion. Little Richard's story illuminates dynamics that still shape Black queer communities today, demonstrating that harmful theological and cultural forces remain active and influential.

title: Decoding Decisions: Folk Theories of Urgent Care Triage Algorithms from Koreatown (K-Town), Los Angeles
abstract: Growing efforts to address algorithmic bias in healthcare have considered increasing data collection methods and model transparency. Yet, this often prioritizes a statistical definition of bias, failing to account for the compounded biases systematic barriers present, particularly for populations who have historically been neglected by the healthcare system. In healthcare, the process in which patients are evaluated and prioritized to receive care, known as triage, is an algorithm which may look different across clinical settings. Understanding how individuals form folk theories (i.e., intuitive and informal theories to explain outcomes of processes and which influence reactions and behavior) about the triage process is significant as it reveals how perceptions of triage algorithms and their potential bias shape access to healthcare through future decision-making. In this project, based in the neighborhood of Koreatown, Los Angeles, 10 interviews with low-income community members from different family generations and an autoethnography by the author, revealed the formation of specific folk theories when seeking urgent care for themselves and/or for a family member. Folk theories included self-presentation of symptoms, awareness of intersectional identities, and perceptions of resource constraints. Additionally, reflections on personal experiences undergoing triage revealed considerations patients make about leaving the waiting room and in some cases, choosing alternative healthcare provider options. This research underscores the importance of folk theories, ones which do not need to be technically accurate, but which nonetheless play a role in informing patients' and their families' decisions about when, how, and whether to seek future care.

title: Post-Colonial Community Perspectives on Cultural Heritage and Archaeology in Corozal, Belize
abstract: How people engage with and understand cultural heritage shapes how it is preserved within communities and how it is understood by broader academic audiences. Heritage is typically described as a tangible or intangible property inherited; however, due to the diverse cultural identities within a Post-Colonial context, Belizean cultural heritage challenges top-down models of heritage management and raises new questions about who benefits from defining and curating heritage sites. This paper asks how community members in Corozal, Belize, perceive and engage with cultural heritage in a Post-Colonial context. Using photos of local heritage sites to facilitate discussions and gather community perspectives on heritage and archaeology fosters an inclusive approach to these topics. A unique understanding of Corozal's current state of cultural heritage and archaeology is created by bringing diverse community voices into conversation with existing literature. Many of the issues discussed by community leaders and scholars centered on disseminating information and on the relationships among the community, community leaders, and archaeologists. Local claims are supported by community discussions, revealing complex relationships between people's engagement with sites and their knowledge of the landscapes' long-term history. Therefore, the community's voices provide a better understanding of how to frame archaeology and heritage efforts in the area.

title: Antisemitism and Anti-Zionism: A Case Study on Jewish Student perspectives at Northwestern University
abstract: This thesis explores how Jewish undergraduate students at Northwestern University understand and navigate the relationship between anti-Zionism and antisemitism. Drawing on 15 semi-structured interviews, I examine how students interpret political discourse, experience campus climate, and make sense of the boundary between legitimate political critique and identity-based harm. This research is important at Northwestern because the university has become a highly visible site of these tensions. Over the past few years, encampments, administrative decisions, and national political attention have made Northwestern an active case study of how these issues unfold. That visibility means students are not only forming their own perspectives, but also reacting to media narratives, federal interventions, and institutional responses that often amplify or distort what they actually experience on the ground. Findings show that students hold a range of perspectives shaped by upbringing, education, and personal connections to Israel. Some maintain a clear distinction between anti-Zionism and antisemitism, while others see them as frequently overlapping, especially when rhetoric generalizes or targets Jewish identity. Antisemitism is often described as indirect, showing up less through explicit incidents and more through discomfort, self-censorship, and uncertainty in campus spaces. Students also express frustration with campus discourse that treats Israel solely as political, overlooking its personal and cultural significance. This disconnect contributes to feeling misunderstood and limits opportunities for nuanced dialogue. By centering Jewish student perspectives when Northwestern is under intense scrutiny, this study highlights how national debates are actually lived on a single campus, and why more thoughtful conversations are needed.

title: Cardiac Synchrony in Co-Rumination Dyads: Using EKG to Study Interpersonal Dysfunction in Depression
abstract: Interpersonal dysfunction, or a reduced capacity to build and maintain social connections, is a significant component of depression. Depressive symptoms, such as withdrawal and disconnection, can be maladaptive, leading to cycles of distress and isolation that further exacerbate these symptoms. One identified marker of interpersonal dysfunction is co-rumination, defined as the excessive discussion of problems and negative emotions within close relationships. The NEAR Lab is currently analyzing data from a co-rumination study, in which friend dyads were recruited to engage in observed naturalistic conversation; in each pair, at least one individual reported difficulties with self-confidence. During these conversations, behavioral, linguistic, and physiological data were collected. The present analysis focuses on the physiological data collected, specifically the cardiac functioning within dyads measured through electrocardiogram (EKG) recordings. Heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), and measures of cardiac synchrony will be assessed to determine the extent to which co-rumination can be detected physiologically. We hypothesize that dyads will exhibit increased cardiac synchrony, reflected by increased heart rate and HRV alignment. Together, these patterns may suggest a physiological component underlying interpersonal dysfunction and co-rumination. Findings will contribute to a growing understanding of how depression is shaped by social interaction and how individual mental illness symptoms may influence members of one's social network.

title: HANDFUL: Dexterous Multi-Step Robot Manipulation with Resource Awareness
abstract: Dexterous robot hands offer rich opportunities for multi-step manipulation: for example, grasping an object and then pushing another object, pulling a drawer, or pressing a button. However, most prior work in dexterous manipulation focuses on single, isolated tasks. In contrast, our key insight is that these multi-step manipulation tasks require resource-aware grasps where the robot must conserve fingers for later actions rather than simply optimizing an initial whole-hand grasp in isolation. We introduce HANDFUL, a learning framework that treats finger usage as a limited resource and rewards the robot for exploring one- and two-finger grasps that leave fingers and in-hand space available for downstream tasks. These grasps are then efficiently selected and trained for downstream tasks via curriculum-based policy learning We further propose HANDFUL-Bench, a simulation benchmark that introduces sequential dexterous manipulation tasks across multiple second-subtask objectives, including pushing, pulling, and pressing, under a shared grasp + second objective setup. Second objectives include: pushing another object, pressing a button, twisting a knob, pulling a drawer, and grasping a second object. Results show that resource-aware grasp planning improves both success rate and robustness compared to a baseline that greedily optimizes the initial grasp before attempting the second subtasks. We additionally validate our approach on a real dexterous hand. Together, this work establishes resource-aware grasp planning as a key principle for multi-step dexterous manipulation. Supplementary material is available on our website: [handful-dex.github.io] (http://handful-dex.github.io).

title: Inafa'maolek Archaeologies: CHamoru heritage resurgence amidst U.S. militarization on Guahan (Guam)
abstract: The rise of U.S. militarization on Guam and the passage of federal laws governing cultural resource management and environmental protection have rapidly increased archaeological surveying over the last few decades. This research investigates the role of CHamorus, the Indigenous people of Guam and the Mariana Islands, who work as archaeologists and historic preservationists to steward Indigenous cultural heritage amidst military build-up. These applied anthropologists play a crucial role in protecting CHamoru heritage, working with archaeological materials spanning up to 4,000 years old that connect present day CHamorus to ancient ancestors. Using ethnographic methods, including participant observation and semi-structured interviews, this research examines how CHamoru archaeologists and historic preservationists are incorporating CHamoru knowledge systems throughout their work on their ancestral homelands, focusing on the newly constructed Marine Corps Camp Blaz base. This research maps the current institutional landscape of heritage management on Guam, identifying some of the challenges of CHamoru archaeologists and historic preservationists within their work. For these practitioners, archaeology has been utilized as a site of resistance towards colonial knowledge production on the CHamoru people. Drawing on Indigenous and activist archaeological literature, this research explores how CHamoru practitioners are subsequently navigating Indigenous identity, community, and place-making as they work on specific heritage sites. By centering CHamoru relationships to land and prioritizing community access, CHamoru practitioners in the field are utilizing archaeology as a tool to foster sovereignty through decolonial heritage education, while simultaneously mobilizing to protect Indigenous cultural landscapes amidst violent militarization.

title: Decoding Cave Wall Patterns to Search for Life Elsewhere
abstract: Caves on Mars and the Moon suggest that similar environments on Earth can help scientists search for signs of life beyond our planet. One promising avenue of research is focused on "biovermiculations" - worm-like patterns of microbe-rich material that form on cave walls. Most studies of these features come from sulfur-rich caves, where microbes drive their formation through sulfur-based chemistry. This study examines biovermiculations in Mammoth Cave, Kentucky, a limestone cave with different environmental conditions, to better understand how they form and whether they are truly biological in origin. Our hypothesis is that biovermiculations in non-sulfur caves are shaped by active microbial processes. We combined microscopy, spatial mapping, and DNA analysis techniques to analyze these patterns. In Mammoth Cave, biovermiculations appear across five distinct morphologies and are made from materials like soot, mud, and cricket guano. Their form is influenced more by the type and behavior of available material than by nearby patterns. Microscopy revealed motile microorganisms that could actively rearrange material on cave surfaces. We also found that these features have developed over at least the past century, growing into 19-20th century soot deposits but not significantly affecting newer ones (post-1970). Genetic analyses show that the microbial communities within biovermiculations are distinct from other sites and share similar compositions across samples. Many of these microbes are associated with sulfur and iron cycling, as well as methane use, suggesting diverse metabolic activity.
