Identifying such redundancies would greatly reduce the problem size, and we therefore propose to break down programs into persistent and non-persistent components, with only the need validate the latter with each new transformation. Therefore, this work enables AI transformation passes to be integrated into compilation pipelines without an overwhelming overhead.

title: Romance and Report Cards: The Effect of Romantic Relationship Commitment on Perceived Academic Performance
abstract: Romantic relationships and academics play significant roles in college students’ lives. However, researchers disagree whether romantic relationships can facilitate or impede a student’s perceived academic success, and most research focuses on GPA, rather than student-reported measures, as a proxy for academic performance. We sought to determine, first, whether the presence of a romantic relationship predicts perceived academic performance, and second, whether the relative seriousness of one’s romantic relationship predicts perceived academic performance. Undergraduate students (N = 78) were surveyed on their romantic relationship status, relationship seriousness, and academic performance through a series of questionnaires. Results indicated that neither the presence of a romantic relationship nor the seriousness of that relationship significantly affected perceived academic performance. Post hoc, we found a significant positive correlation between sleep duration and academic performance, meaning students who reported more hours of sleep felt they performed better academically. A subsequent linear regression analysis (controlling for sleep) suggested that sleep may mediate the relationship between romantic involvement and academic outcomes. Our findings show that students in romantic relationships are not necessarily academically disadvantaged, although students who sleep longer durations are likely academically advantaged. These insights help students balance academic and interpersonal commitments to fulfill their personal goals.

title: Investigating the effects of bioactive peptides on peptide amphiphile nanofibers on an organoid spinal cord injury model
abstract: Spinal cord injury often results in lifelong sensory and motor dysfunction due to the poor regenerative capacity of the central nervous system and the formation of an inhibitory glial scar in the injury site that causes degeneration of white and gray matter. A leading cause for this is the increase of chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs) surrounding the cystic cavity which upon binding to protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) receptors (PTPσ) inhibits regeneration. Interestingly, this roadblock to recovery has been reversed by a membrane-permeable peptide that deactivates PTPσ. Despite this therapeutic potential, the short systemic circulation of these peptides poses a significant clinical burden, requiring daily injections for months after injury. To prolong the bioactive effects of this peptide, a novel system has been developed in which these cell-permeating peptide “sliders” associate dynamically with peptide amphiphile supramolecular nanofibers through electrostatic interactions. This system forms an injectable hydrogel that provides both mechanical support and biological potency to support neuronal growth by prolonging the effects of PTPσ-targeting peptides. Here, we investigate the biological potential and mechanisms of the “sliders” in a clinically translational 3D human organoid model. Through this study, it was discovered that treatment with “sliders” significantly enhanced axonal growth in the sites of injury. It was also discovered that delivery of peptides by peptide amphiphiles were highly specific to the site of injury and showed high levels of cellular internalization. These findings demonstrate the significant potential of the novel “sliders” for future in vivo, and ultimately therapeutic applications.

title: Investigating Motor Thalamus Encoding of Forelimb Muscle Activity in Mice
abstract: The motor thalamus (Mthal) is a key brain structure important for motor learning and motor execution. Mthal influences movement by projecting to the primary motor cortex (M1), a region that plays a primary role in driving muscle activity to generate movement. While evidence suggests that Mthal provides "high-level" direction to M1 that specifies the identity of an upcoming movement (e.g. a reach or a pull), it may also convey "low-level" direction, encoding patterns of muscle activity during movement execution similar to M1. Due to a lack of simultaneous neural and muscle activity recordings, the extent to which Mthal conveys high versus low-level information to M1 is unclear. To address this gap, the Miri lab collected simultaneous Mthal, M1, and muscle activity recordings in mice performing a naturalistic climbing task. Using these recordings, I sought to compare the amount of muscle predictive information conveyed in both Mthal and M1. To do so, I fit ridge regression models, a regularized form of linear regression, to predict muscle activity from past neural activity in either M1 or Mthal. When muscle activity was predicted using equal amounts of neurons in M1 and Mthal, I found that Mthal was similarly predictive of muscle activity as M1. This suggests that Mthal may convey substantially more low-level muscle-activity commands than previously expected. This challenges the current view that Mthal primarily encodes high-level movement and offers new insight into how the brain generates the patterns of muscle activity that underlie movement.

title: Engineering Vascularized Spinal Cord Organoids through Bioactive Peptide Amphiphile-Mediated Vascular Cell Integration
abstract: Organoids are revolutionary miniature human tissue models made from pluripotent stem cells that replicate the native tissue structures and functions of human organs. However, organoids that lack a vascular system for gas and nutritional exchange will eventually experience necrosis or poor differentiation in the interior as they grow larger in size. To address this limit, this project focuses on engineering vascularized spinal cord organoids (SCOs) by integrating vascular cells using bioactive peptide amphiphiles (PAs). In this study, preliminary trials were conducted to determine the optimal concentration and type of bioactive PAs, designed to promote vascular growth and proliferation. Histology markers for proliferation, morphology, and vascular receptor activation determined that the ideal treatment conditions consist of micelle-forming angiogenic PAs and fiber-forming diluent PAs. Following these trials, a 3D co-culture system was established by introducing vascular cells to SCOs. To optimize vascular cell integration and penetration into the organoid core, three distinct PA treatment timelines were examined: two days before vascular cell introduction, simultaneous application with vascular cells, and delayed treatment following co-culture. These co-cultures were maintained for 10 days to monitor the rate of vascular cell integration and proliferation. Results were evaluated through immunostaining and imaging to analyze vascular cell penetration and vascular receptor activation within the SCOs. Our experimental strategies would provide useful insights into vascular engineering in human spinal cord organoids by leveraging the potent bioactivity of PAs. These improved vascular organoid models will facilitate future studies of spinal cord injuries and the development of regenerative therapeutic strategies.

title: What We Say to Ourselves: Inner Speech, Neuroticism, and Psychological Flexibility
abstract: This study examined how neuroticism and psychological flexibility relate to the frequency and content of inner speech, with a focus on clarifying whether these relationships follow a moderation or mediation model. Understanding these links is important because inner speech is closely tied to emotion regulation and mental health, yet the mechanisms connecting personality traits to inner speech remain unclear. A demographically representative sample of adults in the United States was recruited through Prolific. Participants completed self-report questionnaires measuring neuroticism, rumination, psychological flexibility, and different aspects of inner speech, including total frequency and content. We tested both moderation and mediation models to evaluate how these variables are connected. The results did not support a moderation model in which neuroticism changes the effects of inner speech. Instead, findings supported a mediation model: higher neuroticism predicted greater rumination, which in turn was associated with increased total inner speech. There was no evidence for a "for better or worse" effect based on level of neuroticism. Psychological flexibility was not related to total inner speech but was associated with greater positive regulatory inner speech and was only indirectly related to lower rumination through its negative correlation with neuroticism. These findings suggest that total inner speech is largely driven by rumination, while positive regulatory speech reflects a separate process linked to psychological flexibility. This distinction helps refine current models of inner speech and points to different targets for future research and interventions aimed at improving emotional well-being.

title: Modeling Peripheral Artery Disease with Engineered Skeletal Muscle Tissue
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is characterized by arterial blockages that reduce blood flow to the limbs causing nutrient and oxygen deficiencies in skeletal muscles. Of the 200 million people affected worldwide, half experience muscle loss, tissue damage, and declines in mobility and quality of life. PAD research primarily relies on 2D cell cultures, which cannot replicate tissue-level behavior. Engineered muscle tissues (EMTs) overcome this by combining myoblast cells with a hydrogel to recreate the cellular organization and environment of native skeletal muscle tissue, enabling tissue-level observations. Since EMTs can be grown using various hydrogel compositions, we aimed to identify conditions that provided a straightforward and reproducible setup. EMTs were generated on PDMS posts, to simulate muscle attachment between bones, using two hydrogel formulations: (1) 3 U/mg thrombin + 4 mg/mL fibrinogen + 5 mg/mL Matrigel (2) 4.1 mg/mL rat tail type I collagen + 10 mg/mL Matrigel. Surface treatments of posts were also tested to determine effects on cell adhesion and viability. None of these conditions produced EMTs attached to the PDMS posts, although the collagen-based hydrogel successfully assembled as a thin sheet, and was the simplest and most consistent to work with. Future work will involve optimizing PDMS functionalization, characterizing the makeup of the collagen hydrogel using histology, and adding fibroblast cells to improve tissue formation. Optimization of the EMT generation process enables observations that more closely reflect PAD pathology in humans without the cost, time constraints, and ethical concerns associated with animal models.

title: Playing the Supplicant: The Usurpation of Flattery in Shakespeare’s Richard III
abstract: In William Shakespeare's Richard III, the villain, Richard, employs flattery as his method to usurp the throne and rule as a tyrant. Richard's manipulation tactic, flattery, traditionally thought of as a monarch's weakness, is unexpected given the teachings of classical and medieval scholars like Plutarch and Erasmus. Flattery, which according to these thinkers was a vice monarchs were instructed to avoid, becomes a tool for Richard to exploit. My thesis explains why Richard's utilization of flattery, while initially a source of strength in Richard's ascension to the throne, is actually a sign of weakness and instability in his status as a ruler, and in his kingdom more broadly. I analyzed classical, medieval, and modern scholars to understand the significance of flattery within kingship, and more specifically, amongst Shakespeare's monarchs. After close-reading two scenes that, when compared, most capture the shift in flattery as Richard's strength to a symbol of his weakness, I found that it is Richard's status as a usurper that forces him to resort to flattery as a means to obtain the throne. Richard's illegitimate rise to power allows flattery to act as a strength while he works to secure the throne because his ascent is already based on murder and falsities. However, once in power, this unstable foundation of manipulation causes flattery to be an ill-equipped substitute for the paranoia and death that Richard has caused. Framing flattery as Richard's weakness, rather than strength, allows for Richard's tyranny to be more than just a series of murders.

title: Wearable Sweat Sensor for Chronic Kidney Disease Biomarkers
abstract: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a global health burden that affects hundreds of millions of people and strains healthcare systems with rising treatment costs. As the condition advances, clinical severity increases exponentially, yet many individuals remain undiagnosed due to the invasive nature and high cost of traditional blood-based screening. This barrier is particularly evident in low-resource environments where limited clinical infrastructure prevents early intervention. Consequently, there is an urgent need for a cost-efficient, non-invasive early screening tool to identify health changes. Our research compared the concentrations of urea and creatinine biomarkers in sweat and blood using laboratory standards (LC-MS) to establish sweat as a reliable substitute for monitoring kidney health. Next, we developed a wearable colorimetric sensor featuring an on-demand, local sweat stimulation feature and two distinct detection pathways: a pH- compensated system for urea and a spectrophotometric system for creatinine. The device utilizes colorimetric assays for qualitative screening via the naked eye, while color analysis enables quantitative detection of biomarker concentrations. Quantitative validation showed strong linear trends between sweat and blood biomarkers (R2 = 0.89 for creatinine; R2 = 0.79 for urea). This data demonstrates great potential in classifying different stages of CKD, which is vital for early screening. Future work will focus on optimizing colorimetric assay performance and designing user-friendly device form factors for on-human validation to evaluate sensor stability. This innovation aims to empower patients with autonomy and provide accessible screening to improve the quality of life for those at risk of CKD.

title: Sensory Neuron and Mast Cell Interaction in Itch Responses of Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (RDEB)
abstract: Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (RDEB) is an inherited blistering disorder that is characterized by inflammation and severe itch. Our preliminary data showed increased mast cells from the immune system and a specific type of sensory neuron called Mas-related G-protein-coupled receptor D (MrgprD). While MrgprD-expressing neurons are typically involved in itch-related behaviors, their role in RDEB has not been well studied. In normal skin, MrgprD+nerves communicate with mast cells through a molecule called glutamate to reduce their activation, thus reducing excessive skin inflammation. However, in injured tissue, glutamate has been shown to increase inflammatory signaling in mast cells. We hypothesize that RDEB promotes increased MrgprD+ nerve density in the outermost layer of the skin and enhances MrgprD+ interaction with mast cells, contributing to itch and pain. To study this, we used an RDEB mouse model to visualize the nerves and examined their proximity to mast cells in skin and dorsal root ganglia (DRGs), a cluster of neurons responsible for relaying sensory information to the brain. Tissues were stained to identify activated mast cells and imaged for quantitative analysis. This analysis showed a significant 18-fold increase in the density of MrgprD+nerves in the outermost layer of the skin, and these nerves were located significantly closer to mast cells. Additionally, RDEB DRGs had an significant increase in mast cell specific mRNA levels. These results suggest the increase in MrgprD⁺ density and number of mast cells may contribute to the persistent inflammation in RDEB.

title: And Here I Am!” Chronotopic Memories in a Holocaust Survivor's Autobiographical Narratives
abstract: At another family gathering I felt a relative's hands on my cheeks. In awe, he uttered "pontosan ugy nez ki az arcod, mint a dednagyanyade." This Hungarian phrase roughly means that my face looks exactly like my great-grandmother's. I was named after her son and my grandfather, Dr. Leslie Koltai. Along with his name, I inherited recordings of his story. Born in Karcag, a small town in Eastern Hungary, Koltai survived the Holocaust, then became an anti-fascism journalist during the Hungarian Revolution. Later, fearing persecution, he escaped the country and settled in the United States. This thesis analyzes how Holocaust testimonies change over time and how these changes inform self-understanding. Drawing on Bakhtin's theory of the chronotope, a literary device that attends to "space-time" in narrative, I analyze how Koltai's recollections illuminate not only his lived experiences but also processes of sense-making with particular attention to the mobilization of time as a resource. Findings show that temporality serves as a resource for understanding the past in relation to the present and advances a narrator's understanding of the possibilities of the imagined future. However, key aspects of the narrator's understanding of his life experience do not change and are consistent across both tapes. This work demonstrates the importance of recording survivors' second and third testimonials and the value of attending to the holistic nature of the experiences recounted. Future research directions might involve analyzing multiple testimonials from survivors of conflict to show how these experiences are understood by future generations.

title: Potential Protectors of Genomic Stability in Keratinocytes
abstract: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), which originates from keratinocytes in the epidermis, is characterized by the highest mutation rate of any cancer, making it difficult to identify cancer-driving mutations, and develop targeted treatments. Microsatellite instability (MSI) contributes to genomic instability and mutation. Microsatellites are regions in the DNA where a 1-6 base pair sequence repeats many times. During cell division, errors are more common at these sites, but are fixed by DNA repair proteins like MSH6. ACSS2 could potentially preserve genomic stability in keratinocytes, since decreased ACSS2 expression was observed in skin cancer cells. ACSS2 is an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of acetate to acetyl-CoA, to provide a source of acetyl groups for post translational modifications (PTMs) to proteins which alter their functions. MSH6 is a protein that forms a complex which is stabilized by acetylation. To study if ACSS2 maintains microsatellite stability by stabilizing MSH6, shRNA was used to knock down expression of ACSS2. The DNA was then extracted, amplified, and loaded into gels to observe irregular sized DNA fragments, which would indicate MSI. A plasmid, a circular piece of DNA, is also being developed that uses fluorescence to signal the presence of MSI. Fluorescent imaging of keratinocytes infected with the reporter plasmid confirm presence of the fluorescence as expected, but it has yet to be evaluated whether it is due to the presence of MSI. Findings to this project would reveal potential pathways to genomic instability in cSCC, providing a foundation for research for targeted therapies.

title: Simulating the Phase Behavior of Polydisperse DNA-Nanoparticle Systems
abstract: Nanoparticles that are surface-functionalized with DNA strands can act as programmable atom equivalents (PAEs), where the nanoparticle core behaves analogously to an atom and DNA hybridization defines the interparticle interactions. By manipulating PAE sizes and DNA sequences, the PAEs can form crystals with controllable lattice symmetry and nanoparticle spacing. The assembly of polydisperse PAE systems into a single phase has proven to be challenging due to the thermodynamic instability caused by size disparity. Recent experimental attempts have shown some success in single-phase crystallization by introducing flexible spacers within the DNAs to make the effective hydrodynamic radii more similar. However, it is unclear what the limits of the flexible spacers are in overcoming the effects of size disparity. Understanding the phase behavior requires systematic and quantitative analysis, which is extremely challenging experimentally due to the large number of systems that need to be synthesized and investigated. In this work, we construct a phase diagram of polydisperse PAE systems using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with two different models: a colloidal model and a coarse-grained DNA model. These models can provide crucial thermodynamic information with relatively low computational cost. The colloidal model is used to determine the boundaries of the phase diagram, while the coarse-grained model is used to explain any discrepancies with the experimental data and provide a detailed understanding of the thermodynamics of the interactions. In doing so, we explain the effects of nanoparticle core diameter, spacer flexibility, and nanoparticle type on crystallization, and provide guidelines for experimental synthesis.

title: A Rat Model of Neonatal Encephalopathy: Exploring the Effects of Oxygen Deficiency on Central Auditory Function
abstract: Prematurely born infants commonly experience oxygen deficiency due to episodes of asphyxiation before, during, or shortly after birth. This contributes to neonatal encephalopathy, a condition of neurological dysfunction that is linked to hearing loss and other communication impairments. However, the underlying mechanisms of these deficits and their developmental trajectories are poorly understood. Our lab is investigating the impact of oxygen deficiency on auditory function depending on age of exposure and oxygen reduction magnitude. We used auditory brainstem response (ABR) testing to evaluate 21-day-old rat pups who were exposed to 10 minutes of anoxic (&1% oxygen) or normative (~21% oxygen) treatment on two consecutive days. Another group of pups was exposed to 11% oxygen to assess the effects of milder oxygen reduction. ABRs with 4, 8, 16, and 32 kHz tone burst stimuli were processed using an automated R-script and peak I-III latencies were compared between and within groups. When pups were exposed to anoxia at birth and postnatal day 1, 100% survived and preliminary analysis revealed delayed latencies at 8 kHz in comparison to the control and 11% oxygen groups. However, when pups were exposed at postnatal day 6, 100% died and ABRs were unobtainable. These results suggest that a greater magnitude of oxygen reduction amplifies the detrimental impacts of oxygen deficiency on neurological and auditory processes, but further experimentation is needed to understand the role of exposure age. Our findings may also clarify the implications of preterm births on hearing and communication development.

title: Dilute Plasmonic Copper Alloys: Leveraging Surface Engineering for Enhanced Catalysis
abstract: Modern catalysis is increasingly focused on making chemical processes more sustainable, including using light as an energy source. Dilute plasmonic alloys are a promising class of materials for this purpose. These nanoparticles smaller than the wavelength of light combine a light-responsive metal with small amounts of a catalytically active metal, allowing them to both absorb light and drive chemical reactions. Systems such as copper–platinum and copper–rhodium have shown promise for propane dehydrogenation, an important reaction that produces propylene, a key industrial chemical. However, replacing expensive metals with more abundant, non-precious alternatives remains a major challenge. Here, we study copper–cobalt nanoparticles as a low-cost alternative. We synthesize 2– 3 nm particles and show that their surface composition changes depending on the surrounding gas and temperature. Using solid-state infrared spectroscopy (Diffuse Reflectance Infrared Fourier Transform Spectroscopy), we find that hydrogen pushes cobalt below the surface, while carbon monoxide at 150 °C and oxygen at 350 °C pull cobalt to the surface, properties that are consistent with theoretical properties of cobalt, and are accompanied by an initial enhancement in catalytic rates with surface cobalt. These shifts are reversible and stable over time. These surface changes are also linked to changes in catalytic activity, suggesting that the active sites can be tuned by controlling reaction conditions. This work demonstrates that copper–cobalt nanoparticles can serve as a model system for designing catalysts with adjustable active sites. More broadly, it highlights the potential of earth-abundant materials for efficient and controllable catalytic processes.

title: Territorial Membership: U.S. Naturalization Law and Defining Who Can Be American, 1897-1938
abstract: This study investigates how federal judges decided on eligibility for citizenship for people in US territories and what rationales they employed to justify their decisions. This work expands the criteria of Ian Haney-López’s book, White by Law, in which he investigates how race is legally defined through naturalization cases. Haney-López limits his study to cases where race is the sole deciding factor for citizenship as opposed to territorial status, procedural complications, or jurisdiction. However, expanding his criteria to consider how judges reasoned through both territorial status and race is important because it highlights how legal racial boundaries in the United States were reconfigured as the U.S. empire expanded. To identify patterns in legal reasoning, I read and coded decisions from eighteen naturalization cases and compared my codes to those of another coder. We then compared the case decisions and justifications with the territorial status of the petitioner. Our analysis revealed that when there is an ambiguous territorial status and no legal precedent, judges speculate the intentions Congress had when writing the naturalization acts. Furthermore, stemming from contradictory acts of Congress, judges scrutinized particular jurisdictions such as the Philippines. This study has implications for the sociolegal understanding of how citizenship status and eligibility is understood in the United States empire. Our study suggests that definitions of race, territorial status and naturalization eligibility that were legally restrictive created systems of racially discriminatory exclusion from naturalization, or discriminatory social ideas of who could be American for the petitioners studied.

title: First-Year Transition Programs: an X Factor for the FGLI College Experience
abstract: In PhD candidate Rebecca Lawrence's study, she explores the relationship between participation in first-year transition programs (FYTPs) and mental well-being among first-generation/low-income (FGLI) students of color. She interviewed a group of students who participated in a three-week FYTP at a highly selective, predominantly white institution (PWI) and a non-FYTP control group. The FYTP aims to help FGLI students acclimate to university life both socially and academically through mini-courses, mentoring, and resource workshops. This study addresses persistent feelings of alienation among FGLI students and examines how the FYTP supports belonging and mental health outcomes. As an Emerging Scholar, I cleaned transcripts, conducted thematic coding, and wrote summary memos to identify trends in student experiences. These trends would inform FYTP coordinators of areas for improvement while also encouraging other institutions to implement bridge programs for incoming students. Our findings show how, compared to the non-FYTP control group, participants reported stronger support systems, a more critical reception to general orientation, and improved academic adjustment. This work reveals the importance of comprehensive FYTPs for FGLI students. By fostering social networks in which FGLI students connect with each other and preparing students academically, FYTPs may soften the potential whiplash of transitioning to college. The findings suggest that implementing FGLI bridge programs and continuing support for students even after the program's completion, may improve equity and student outcomes across institutions.

title: Romance and Report Cards: The Effect of Romantic Relationship Commitment on Perceived Academic Performance
abstract: Romantic relationships and academics play significant roles in college students’ lives. However, researchers disagree whether romantic relationships can facilitate or impede a student’s perceived academic success, and most research focuses on GPA, rather than student-reported measures, as a proxy for academic performance. We sought to determine, first, whether the presence of a romantic relationship predicts perceived academic performance, and second, whether the relative seriousness of one’s romantic relationship predicts perceived academic performance. Undergraduate students (N = 78) were surveyed on their romantic relationship status, relationship seriousness, and academic performance through a series of questionnaires. Results indicated that neither the presence of a romantic relationship nor the seriousness of that relationship significantly affected perceived academic performance. Post hoc, we found a significant positive correlation between sleep duration and academic performance, meaning students who reported more hours of sleep felt they performed better academically. A subsequent linear regression analysis (controlling for sleep) suggested that sleep may mediate the relationship between romantic involvement and academic outcomes. Our findings show that students in romantic relationships are not necessarily academically disadvantaged, although students who sleep longer durations are likely academically advantaged. These insights help students balance academic and interpersonal commitments to fulfill their personal goals.

title: Toward Autonomous Breathing: Predicting CO2 in Children with CCHS Using Wearable Sensors
abstract: Breathing is something that most people rarely think about, seamlessly adapting to changes in sleep, exercise, or everyday movement. But for children with Congenital Central Hypoventilation Syndrome (CCHS), this automatic control is impaired, requiring reliance on assisted ventilation to breathe. Advances such as phrenic nerve stimulation have enabled patients to live longer and more active lives by restoring diaphragm function. However, these systems still depend on manual, clinician-driven adjustments, limiting their ability to respond in real time to changing metabolic demands. This project investigates whether a patient's ventilatory needs can be anticipated before physiological signals reflect these changes. Transcutaneous CO2 (tcCO2), a key clinical measure of ventilation, is inherently delayed due to physiological and diffusion constraints, restricting its use in real-time control. To address this, we developed a predictive framework using noninvasive wearable signals. We built upon an existing sensing platform and designed an experimental protocol to capture interactions between ventilation and activity. Using synchronized expired CO2 (etCO2) and accelerometry data, we trained a machine learning model (CNN to biLSTM) to learn these physiological patterns. The model was able the identify the delay between signals and predict future CO2 levels with mean absolute errors of 0.55-0.58 mmHg. These results demonstrate the feasibility of predicting clinically meaningful CO2 dynamics from wearable data, providing a foundation for closed-loop, anticipatory control of phrenic nerve stimulation. Future work will focus on building a large, diverse physiological dataset across individuals, enabling personalized and adaptive respiratory support across age, activity level, and patient variability.

title: Living and Learning: Exploring the influence of place on students' communication about climate change across time during a local field trip
abstract: Local environmental education is important to discussions about the future of our climate, which can be overwhelming for students. As the climate changes, every community will encounter unique challenges affecting their lives, so we should incorporate relevant environmental information into educational content. Thus, this project explored place-based learning in an informal context through a study of fifth and sixth grade students' reflections on a field trip about marine ecosystem change in the Gulf of Maine. To investigate how place influences students' discussion of environmental phenomena, transcript coding was used to categorize and quantify the words students used. Independent-samples t-tests and one-way ANOVAs were used to compare word types between school locations and across three school years. A subset of transcripts was also considered qualitatively to identify key themes students discussed. Word use varied significantly more between coastal and inland schools than between urban and rural schools. Inland groups spoke more frequently and used more data analysis and marine species words. Students who used emotional language also used more data analysis terms. Equipping middle school students with the tools to understand and communicate scientific concepts may better prepare the next generation to address specific local effects of climate change. Furthermore, by understanding smaller-scale concepts, students can better recognize their role in the broad scope of climate change. This research shows the potential benefits of considering student identity and place on learning about the environment in informal settings.

title: Renaissance Mythological Afterlives: Transgressing Allusionary Bounds of the Lovers/Victims of Jove's Desire
abstract: Helen, the face who launched a thousand ships, is a figure who emerges in Homer but endures into the English Renaissance. Shakespeare, Marlowe, Jonson, and their English Renaissance drama contemporaries overflow with allusions to female mythological figures. Renaissance drama's classical connection has provoked scholarship for decades, but the comparative study of allusions to mythological women, and particularly the human female targets of Jove's (Jupiter's) violent and deceptive desire, is an under-researched topic that I addressed with my comparative literary analysis of allusions to four lovers/victims of Jove: Danae, Europa, Leda, and Semele. Lovers/victims is a hybrid term that I coined to encompass the divergent, paradoxical characterizations these female figures take up in classical mythology as lovers of Jove and also victims of his violating, omnipotent desire. Through reading the story of the lovers/victims in classical corpus in tandem with the allusions to the lovers/victims across a broad sample of Renaissance drama, I found that female characters in Renaissance drama engage in a conflict-ridden conversation with these classical allusions that embody patriarchal expectations of female embodiment. This point of conflict leads to the emergence of a different form of female subjectivity that emphasizes transformation, both of speech and embodiment. This project presents a new framework for viewing female subjectivity in Renaissance drama that acknowledges these classical allusions not as mythological background noise, but as a foundational place where female embodiment emerges differently in literature and culture itself through a dialectical conversation with the classically-constrained past.

title: Elucidation of Urethane Exchange Mechanism with DABCO
abstract: Thermoset polyurethanes (PUs) are commonly used for applications such as insulation and seat cushions. However, these polymers contain chemical cross-links that make them difficult to recycle through traditional recycling methods. To allow for PU reprocessing in a feasible and scalable manner, dynamic cross-links have been introduced to thermoset PUs, forming PU covalent adaptable networks (CANs). Previous works have found that residual catalysts from the production of commercial PUs, such as 1,4-diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane (DABCO), can catalyze dynamic urethane exchange reactions, thereby creating PU CANs directly from post-consumer waste. By understanding the mechanism of DABCO-catalyzed urethane exchange, we can gain control over the bond exchange reactions and optimize reprocessing for different PU products. To investigate how DABCO-catalyzed PU CANs undergo bond exchange, I conducted a small molecule study which modeled urethane exchange in the presence of DABCO and excess alcohol. When a small amount of alcohol was added, increasing the concentration of alcohol accelerated the rate of DABCO-catalyzed urethane exchange. However, at higher free alcohol concentrations, the catalytic activity of DABCO was inhibited. I observed an initial period with a slow reaction rate, suggesting that an activated catalyst is formed. I found that urea, a side product created from the reaction between urethane and trace water, caused the reaction to exhibit behaviors consistent with the observed initial period. Since commercial PUs contain a wide variety of urethane, urea, and alcohol groups, I hope to apply these fundamental findings to better reprocess post-consumer PU waste.

title: Hunger and Learning: How Food Deserts and Food Insecurity Shape Academic Success
abstract: In Chicago, one in five households with children experiences food insecurity, and over half a million residents live in neighborhoods designated as food deserts (Gallagher, 2006; Greater Chicago Food Depository). This mixed-methods honors thesis investigates the relationship between food access and academic success among school-age children and college students. Quantitative analyses use Chicago Public Schools data from 2018-2019 and U.S. Department of Agriculture food access data to test whether low access to nutritious food predicts academic success. Linear regression models explore associations between food desert prevalence and academic indicators, controlling for poverty and racial composition across neighborhoods. Complementing these analyses, ten in-depth interviews with Northwestern students who have experienced food insecurity provide qualitative insights into the lived experiences of student hunger. Interviews reveal how food insecurity affects energy levels, emotional wellbeing, and concentration, and how intersecting identities-such as race, class, and immigrant status-shape these experiences. Results are expected to demonstrate that residing in areas of low food access correlates with lower rates academic success and that students' narratives underscore the long-term educational consequences of food insecurity. By integrating statistical and narrative data, this study illuminates how structural inequalities in food access reinforce educational disparities and highlights the urgent need for policies addressing both nutritional and academic support for food-insecure youth.

title: Race and Real Estate: Nathan William MacChesney and the Consequential Establishment of Northwestern's Streeterville Campus
abstract: This project examines the history of Northwestern University's medical schools' move to Streeterville in the 1920s and the enduring consequences for both the city's landscape and the institution's development. The relocation from the South Side was not merely logistical, but strategic, positioning Northwestern as a foundational presence in what became some of the most valuable real estate in Chicago. As the catalyst of this move, Nathan William MacChesney, Northwestern Board of Trustees member and prominent Chicago lawyer, is the research focus. Using archives from the McCormick Library and the Chicago History Museum, this study uses Board of Trustees meeting minutes, correspondence involving the Chicago campus, published writings and addresses of MacChesney, and Sanborn fire insurance maps to trace the physical transformation of the Near North Side. These sources reveal MacChesney's extensive influence in the relocation and in shaping the surrounding area. MacChesney's role extended beyond university planning into developing restrictive covenants, private legal agreements used to enforce racial segregation, and eugenic thought and criminological institutions. Archival evidence indicates likely self-dealing in his promotion of University land purchases adjacent to his own property. The recent opening of a new Northwestern Medicine clinic in Bronzeville marks a return to the South Side, providing a contemporary moment to reflect on the origins and implications of this earlier move. By situating Northwestern's expansion within these broader systems, this project contributes to conversations about how institutions reckon with complex histories, highlighting the entanglement of educational growth, urban development, and racial inequality.

title: Projecting the Public: A Framework for Constructing Empirical Visualization Studies of Broader Audiences
abstract: Since the early 2000s, researchers have called for extending studies of how people engage with visualizations to broader, non-expert audiences, yet existing frameworks for designing such studies were built largely for domain experts. Broader-audience work currently represents only 2.1% of recent visualization publications, and studying these audiences poses distinct challenges that existing methodology fails to address, raising the question: What conceptual framework can help researchers design broader-audience visualization studies while anticipating the realities of doing so? To address this gap, we systematically reviewed 73 visualization research papers published between 2020 and 2024 across four premier venues, then conducted 15 semi-structured interviews with authors of such studies, asking researchers to describe their study design decisions, aspirations, and tradeoffs. Reflexive thematic analysis of transcripts revealed a persistent pattern of aspirations versus practical reality. From this, we derived two outputs: a three-part framework for constructing empirical visualization studies, namely (1) casting an audience into a study sample, (2) constructing an experimental setting to study participants in, and (3) capturing how audiences respond and engage, alongside a detailed account of researcher-described gaps between aspiration and reality for each element; e.g., broader recruitment created design tensions, while realistic settings introduced unexpected tradeoffs. Unlike prior frameworks built for specific and controlled domains, our framework addresses the challenges that broader-audience research demands, supporting a visualization research community that designs for diversity of experience and expertise, meets audiences in real-world contexts, and remains transparent about the practical limits of any individual study.

title: Recognition without Responsiveness: Comparing the Turkish-Armenian and Armenian-American Communities
abstract: This thesis examines how classificatory systems shape political possibilities for ethnic minorities by comparing Armenian minorities in the United States and Turkey. Drawing on constructivist theories put forth by Rogers Brubaker, Ian Hacking, and Michel Foucault, this project analyzes how distinct regimes - American multiculturalism and Turkish nationalism - produce convergent outcomes of political marginalization for the Armenian ethnic community. This comparative study is based on 14 semi-structured interviews with American-Armenians conducted over Zoom with participants from across the U.S. and 14 interviews with Turkish-Armenians conducted in-person in Istanbul. Interviews were supplemented with ethnographic observations, secondary sources in Armenian studies, and archival research. In the U.S., Armenian-American legal classification as "white" enabled integration and institutional success for early Armenian immigrants, but renders current Armenian-American foreign policy claims as narrow ethnic interest demands. This limits policy success beyond symbolic recognition. In Turkey, Armenians are officially recognized as a religious minority under the Treaty of Lausanne, allowing for institutions to remain alive and functioning. However, suppression of ethnic identity and the criminalization of genocide discourse constrain open political advocacy. Across both contexts, recognition operates less as a form of political responsiveness than as a mechanism that limits political voice. These findings challenge the assumption that recognition leads to accountability, showing that classificatory regimes can shape whether states aptly respond to the minority communities they claim to represent.

title: Basal Body Temperature as a Noninvasive Marker of Menstrual Onset and Hormonal Dynamics in Adolescents
abstract: Pubertal hormone surges play a crucial role in adolescent brain development; however, few neuroimaging studies account for neuroendocrine factors in their experimental design and analyses. This is largely due to methodological gaps related to reliability, cost, and invasiveness of traditional approaches. Basal body temperature has recently emerged as a potential proxy for hormonal shifts in adult menstrual cycles, yet this approach has not yet been validated in adolescents. This study investigates whether continuous body temperature tracking can serve as a noninvasive marker of hormonal fluctuations in adolescent females. Data were drawn from a longitudinal neuroimaging study conducted by the Child and Adolescent Translational Science lab in adolescents (N = 4; F; age = 14.9 1.3 years). Nightly distal body temperature was recorded via Oura Ring, and saliva samples were collected over 5-7 weeks and analyzed for estradiol, progesterone, and testosterone concentrations. This study investigates whether fluctuations in temperature over time predict the onset of menstruation compared to self-reported dates, and whether a correlation exists between physiological and hormonal signals. Preliminary analysis revealed that hysteresis-based temperature modeling accurately predicted menses onset in an initial participant. Further analyses will investigate whether predictive accuracy can be generalized across participants of varying ages and menstrual cycle regularity. These findings suggest the possibility for continuous temperature tracking in offering a noninvasive and scalable method for capturing pubertal hormone dynamics, opening new pathways for ecologically valid measurements of adolescent development in endocrine research.

title: Hyperparameter Tuning in Causal ML Models: The Bayesian vs. Frequentist Approach
abstract: Machine learning's predictive power and flexibility have driven its integration with econometric methods, giving rise to the field of causal machine learning (causal ML), which focuses on estimating treatment effects in complex, high-dimensional settings. Despite promising advances, empirical applications of causal ML remain constrained by underexplored challenges in model configuration, particularly hyperparameter tuning, which is frequently ad hoc and inadequately studied. This thesis investigates whether Bayesian hyperparameter tuning outperforms standard automatic tuning methods in causal ML applications, using the X-learner as a framework for estimating conditional average treatment effects (CATEs). The analysis distinguishes two sequential objectives: a tuning stage, in which hyperparameters are selected to minimize cross-validated predictive error, and an evaluation stage, in which models are assessed on the accuracy of treatment effect estimation. The central question is whether predictive gains achieved through Bayesian tuning in the first stage translate into improved causal estimation in the second. Results confirm that Bayesian tuning yields consistent predictive improvements over automatic methods, consistent with the broader ML literature. However, evidence that these gains translate to more accurate treatment effect estimation is lacking, revealing a disconnect between the tuning and evaluation stages. This disconnect reflects a fundamental misalignment between the internal processes that guide ML model development and the primary objective of causal inference frameworks. As ML methods become more deeply integrated with econometric frameworks, aligning internal model metrics with causal estimation objectives emerges as a critical direction for future research.

title: Quantification, Spatial Analysis, and Source Attribution of Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) in Chicago Soils
abstract: Polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are a carcinogenic class of persistent organic pollutants found ubiquitously in soils. While a background survey of PAHs in the soil of the city of Chicago was conducted two decades ago, it lacked analysis of emission sources and human health risks, had poor resolution, and does not reflect the modernization of the city. This study assesses contemporary PAH contamination levels and distribution in Chicago's public green spaces to determine current sources of contamination and associated exposure risks. Seventy-six soil samples were collected from 22 different community areas and analyzed via microwave-assisted extraction and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to quantify 16 PAH congeners. Results reveal that 97% of samples exceed residential soil screening levels set by the EPA for at least one carcinogenic PAH congener. Significant spatial gradients show samples adjacent to major arterial roadways have higher concentrations of PAHs. Source diagnostic ratios identify fossil fuel combustion, mainly from vehicular traffic, as the dominant source of contamination across the city. These findings suggest that, though modern vehicular traffic poses health risks to the citizens of Chicago through its atmospheric emissions of PAHs, the soil of Chicago's parks and public spaces acts as a contaminant sink and additional avenue for human exposure. These results provide an updated baseline of PAH contamination and demonstrate how industrial and vehicular fuel combustion contribute to environmental contamination and ultimately affect human health.

title: Potential of AI Research Tool NotebookLM in Journalism
abstract: For journalists, answers to investigative questions are often hidden in extensive archives, poorly photocopied or complicated by archaic language. Archives can provide context for current topics; however, the process of digging through archives is time consuming and tedious, especially when journalists have to break urgent news. NotebookLM, powered by Google Gemini, is a closed-source AI tool that conducts note-taking and research. Contrary to open models like ChatGPT, NotebookLM only produces responses from the sources it's given, like publication archives. This study investigates the potential of using NotebookLM to maximize research efficiency for journalists. Using 20th-century issues of The Times, the study simulates common background research tasks in journalism- building timelines of events, summarizing detailed stories, and tracking the appearances of people and organizations across archives- to test how well NotebookLM can extract precise information from complex archival content. This examination reveals that while the AI tool can create coherent overviews and paraphrased summaries of stories, inaccurate or "hallucinated" outputs of data are an ongoing challenge with NotebookLM. Despite these accuracy issues, NotebookLM's ability to denote underlying sources does enable relatively quick fact-checking of AI responses, so the tool may still be useful to save time when processing large archives of information. When directing urgent and in-depth investigations, journalists must feel that they can use an AI tool in confidence. These findings from a research assistant in the School of Communication's Computational Journalism Lab are a first step toward understanding how journalists can best incorporate AI into their professional practices.

title: Evaluating Human Pose Estimation Models in a Hospitalized Patient Population
abstract: Monitoring activity in patients hospitalized on neurological services can be crucial for timely detection of conditions such as falls, delirium, and epilepsy, but remains labor-intensive. Continuous video-based monitoring using pose estimation models offers a scalable alternative to optimize clinical assessments. Model performance in clinical populations, where variable postures and complex environments pose unique challenges, remains unexplored. Three state-of-the-art pre-trained pose estimation models, YOLOv11, OpenPose, and MMPose, were evaluated in hospitalized patients undergoing video-EEG. Each model generated coordinates and confidence scores for facial and body keypoints. From each video, ten frames were randomly selected and manually annotated (17 common keypoints) as ground truth and used to define model-specific confidence thresholds. Sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and ROC curves were computed. Keypoint accuracy was calculated using Euclidean distance between ground truth and model detections. We analyzed 46 videos from 24 hospitalized patients with diverse racial backgrounds. OpenPose showed the highest AUC in 52% of cases (24/46) and highest overall balanced accuracy (BA) of 72% (53% sensitivity, 89% specificity). OpenPose performed better for facial detection (BA 77%, 64%, 90%), while MMPose performed better for upper body (BA 74%, 62%, 85%) and lower body (BA 66%, 48%, 82%). Distance errors were smaller for facial keypoints than for other keypoints. State-of-the-art computer vision models face challenges when applied to clinical videos. Accuracy was highest for facial keypoints and lowest for lower body keypoints. Enhancing performance for neurological inpatients may require custom models trained on clinical datasets or novel, potentially combined, approaches.

title: Bispecific Lipid Vesicles for Controlled Cargo Release and Enhanced Immunotherapy
abstract: Natural Killer (NK) cells are part of our immune system and mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity through CD16 (FcghRIII), allowing clearance of cancer cells. However, upon activation, CD16 is cleaved from the NK cell surface via the ADAM17 metalloprotease, reducing cytotoxic activity. Inhibition of ADAM17 via TNF Protease Inhibitor 2 (TAPI-2) has been shown to block shedding of CD16 and enhance NK cell activity. However, as ADAM17 is present on many cell types, this approach lacks cellular specificity. We hypothesized that bispecific lipid vesicles encapsulating TAPI-2 could enable activation-dependent local inhibition of CD16 cleavage in addition to increasing cancer cell lysis. Vesicles were engineered with surface-conjugated CD16 and HER2 antibodies via SNAP and Halo tags to promote simultaneous engagement of NK cells and HER2+ cancer cells. We proposed that NK cell activation through CD16 engagement leads to perforin release, inducing vesicle membrane permeability and localized TAPI-2 release, therefore inhibiting ADAM17-mediated CD16 shedding. Using flow cytometry, we evaluated CD16 surface expression on NK cells following receptor activation in the presence of soluble TAPI-2 or TAPI-2 encapsulated bispecific vesicles. TAPI-2 presence significantly reduced CD16 shedding relative to controls. Ongoing studies are assessing the impact of TAPI-2 encapsulated bispecific vesicles on cancer cell lysis. This research introduces a vesicular platform to enhance NK cell cytotoxicity and activity, as well as increase cancer cell lysis, by coupling cancer-specific activation and localized inhibition of CD16 cleavage, proposing a novel synthetic biology strategy to enhance NK cell-mediated cancer cell lysis.

title: How Children's Health Insurance Reduces Crime: The Role of Behavioral Health Services in Medicaid
abstract: The United States spends nearly $300 billion annually on the criminal justice system and $140 billion on children's Medicaid. Understanding whether childhood health insurance can reduce adulthood crime - and how - could reshape how policymakers think about both programs. This thesis investigates the mechanisms by which childhood Mediacid eligibility reduces adult criminal behavior. Using variation in state Medicaid eligibility rules across birth cohorts from 1981 to 1984, I estimate the effect of childhood health insurance access on adult arrest rates from FBI data. I then test three possible channels - improved education, reduced financial stress, and better access to behavioral health services - across national datasets covering education, income, mental health, and substance abuse treatment. Each additional year of childhood Medicaid eligibility substantially reduces adult drug and violent arrest rates, with the strongest effects emerging from eligibility during adolescence. Education and financial stress channels show largely insignificant results. Instead, the evidence points to behavioral health as the primary pathway where adolescent substance abuse treatment admissions roughly triple with each additional year of eligibility. These findings suggest that Medicaid reduces crime not by improving schooling or financial outcomes, but by connecting at-risk youth to mental health and substance abuse services during critical developmental windows. This points to Medicaid as both a health investment and a long-run public safety investment.

title: State Supreme Court Selection Mechanisms and Dissent
abstract: Partisan judicial selection reforms occurring across states raise concerns among scholars over judicial independence, yet existing measures that rely on dissent rates as an expression of judicial independence inadequately capture how justices dissent. This study employs mixed-methods to examine the relationship between selection mechanisms, dissent frequency, and the rhetorical content of dissents across state supreme courts. A synthetic control analysis of North Carolina's 2018 transition to partisan elections finds no reliable effect on dissent frequency. Yet a computational textual analysis of 72,480 state supreme court dissents between 1965 and 2019 finds that rhetoric varies across selection mechanisms: partisan-elected courts associated with the most ideologically concordant language, followed by nonpartisan-elected courts, retention courts, and appointment systems. Court composition partly mediates this pattern, as partisan elections that homogenize benches correspond with less ideologically discrepant rhetoric. These findings raise questions about whether mechanisms promoting ideological unity or diversity better foster judicial independence.

title: Potential New Regulators of Body Axis Formation in a Regenerating Marine Worm
abstract: The marine worm Hofstenia miamia has the ability to fully regenerate from virtually any injury, making it a powerful model organism for studying regeneration mechanisms. An important prerequisite for this regenerative ability is the maintenance of signaling gradients that act as a body-wide coordinate system, constantly informing cells of their location within the organism. This coordinate system is essential for measuring the extent of missing tissue following injury and determining which tissues must be regenerated. Though the Wnt signaling gradient is known to govern anterior-posterior (AP) patterning, recently the gene isthmin-like (isml) has been shown to play a role in AP patterning and may be a novel regulator of Wnt signaling. To further investigate isml function, we used RNA interference (RNAi) to knock down isml, finding that this produced a "double-tail" phenotype in regenerating worms. This is similar to RNAi of notum, a known Wnt antagonist. Additionally, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) allowed us to visualize isml mRNA expression, revealing that it is concentrated in the tail tip of the animal. Double FISH of Wnt and isml revealed colocalization in some cells, suggesting that isml may regulate the Wnt signaling gradient. Additionally, AlphaFold predicts that human Isthmin and Notum proteins may bind. This suggests that isml may regulate Wnt signaling through enhancement of Notum, and this mechanism may be conserved in humans. Hyperactive Wnt signaling promotes formation of human cancers. If Isthmin proteins are found to be novel regulators of the Wnt pathway, they could be manipulated for therapeutic purposes.

title: Style Guide: Guiding the Institution and Beyond
abstract: The need for updated, student-centered style guides in journalism is increasingly important as reporting standards evolve across platforms, identities, and subject areas; under the guidance of my mentor, Elise K. De Los Santos, this project considers how institutional guides, such as the Medill Stylebook, can better reflect the broader ecosystem of journalistic standards rather than function as static, standalone resources. As an emerging scholar, I approached this question by developing a structured database of existing style guides, organizing them into three categories: affinity-specific, medium-specific (such as photography and writing), and general or topic-specific guides. I analyzed each guide for accessibility, public availability, and relevance to current industry practices, while also documenting how guides reference and build upon one another. This process revealed that no style guide operates independently; instead, they are deeply interconnected, frequently drawing from shared language and frameworks, suggesting that institutional guides benefit from aligning with this larger body of work. The project also resulted in a comprehensive, organized record of these relationships and a system for tracking updates over time. Taken together, this approach points toward a more sustainable way of maintaining style guides as evolving documents, while making them more accessible and usable for students who may not engage directly with multiple external sources, and reinforcing the role of institutional frameworks within a continuously developing field.

title: Greenland's earliest ecosystems after the last glaciation: Younger Dryas and early Holocene leaf wax analysis
abstract: The Greenland Ice Sheet is shrinking due to anthropogenic climate change, which may dramatically alter ecosystem dynamics, especially in the Northern Hemisphere. During the last deglaciation 12,900 years ago, rapid melting of the Laurentide ice sheet abruptly reversed Earth's warming trend and returned northern regions to near-glacial conditions for over a thousand years. This event, termed the Younger Dryas (YD), is known for its severe temperature decrease, but less is known about its impacts on vegetation and hydrology. My project studies a Greenland lake sediment core spanning the last 13,000 years to analyze the environmental impacts of YD cooling. Lipid biomarkers from leaf waxes are well-preserved in lake sediments throughout time and are therefore used as records of the surrounding landscape. Leaf wax compositions are linked to vegetation source, productivity, and hydrology. Using these properties as paleoproxies, results show a sudden shift to an arid climate at the start of the YD, which stabilizes quickly to higher precipitation conditions after the YD termination. In contrast, regional vegetation productivity is low throughout the YD and is not reestablished until ~800 years post-YD, indicating a gradual landscape development to suitable growing conditions. This ~10.9 kya mark also displays a drastic vegetation turnover similar to a nearby lake which exhibits a shift from herb tundra to a more diverse dwarf shrub heath comparable to modern landscapes. Understanding these differing impacts and recovery timescales from the YD is crucial for contextualizing this extreme climate event in the view of current ice sheet loss.

title: Application of Red Fluorescent PLGA Microspheres for Quantitative Assessment of Pediatric Aspiration
abstract: Pediatric aspiration is a clinically significant condition that can lead to chronic lung injury, infection, and long-term respiratory complications, yet current diagnostic methods such as videofluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) and fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) remain largely qualitative and do not quantify aspiration severity. This project aimed to address this gap by developing a microsphere-based approach to enable quantitative assessment of aspiration. Red fluorescent poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) microspheres were used as surrogate tracers to model aspirated material due to their biocompatibility, controlled size, and improved detectability compared to free dyes. The use of red fluorescence was selected to reduce interference from natural tissue autofluorescence in the airway. The system was evaluated across multiple experimental models, including fixed pig trachea, fresh murine lung and tracheal tissue, and a New Zealand rabbit airway perfusion model to simulate aspiration under physiologically relevant conditions. Known concentrations of microspheres were introduced to assess detectability and quantifiability across conditions. Results demonstrated that microspheres could be reliably detected and quantified in fresh tissue, with higher concentrations producing clear, countable signals and improved signal-to-background contrast. These findings support the feasibility of using microspheres as quantitative tracers for aspiration and establish a foundation for correlating particle distribution with aspiration severity. This approach has the potential to improve diagnostic precision, enable objective severity grading, and support better clinical decision-making in the management of pediatric aspiration.

title: Nitrogen-nitrogen bond formation via electrochemistry
abstract: Many clinically approved drugs contain N-N bonds. Yet, directly bonding two electron-rich nitrogen atoms defies the conventional reactivity pattern because most reactions take place between an electron-rich molecule (nucleophile) and an electron-deficient one (electrophile). For that reason, existing strategies for N-N bond formation often involve the formation of transient electron-deficient nitrogen intermediates. However, these approaches generally require at least one planar, sp2-hybridized nitrogen source. N-N coupling between two non-planar, sp3-hybridized nitrogen atoms is rare, with few reported examples and limited structural diversity. Additionally, these systems often undergo competing decomposition due to weak adjacent carbon-hydrogen bonds. This project employs electrochemistry to remove an electron (oxidize) from the nitrogen atom of a bicyclic compound known as quinuclidine, generating an sp3-hybridized nitrogen radical. Notably, quinuclidine radical avoids the typical decomposition pathway due to its structural constraints. The intermediate is also electrophilic, thereby overcoming the issue with polarity mismatch and reacting readily with nucleophilic nitrogen partners to form N-N bonds. Under the optimized electrochemical condition, oxidized quinuclidine couples with its electron-rich, unoxidized counterpart to produce a doubly positively charged N-N bonded dimer in high yield. This product can be further diversified through ring-opening reactions with oxygen-, nitrogen-, and sulfur-based reagents, providing access to a diverse set of highly functionalized molecules. Overall, this work provides a new route to medicinally relevant N(sp3)-N(sp3) bonded structures that have previously been difficult to synthesize.

title: Chemically Induced Dynein Relocalization in C. elegans Disrupts Faithful Meiosis
abstract: The formation of healthy egg (reproductive) cells depends on a special type of cell division called meiosis. During this process, cells build a structure called the spindle to separate chromosomes. Unlike most cells, egg cells lack typical organizing centers for this structure, making it less clear how the spindle forms and functions properly. This project focuses on dynein, a motor protein that helps move components within the cells along microtubules, which serve as tracks for chromosome movement. Because dynein is found in multiple parts of the spindle, we asked whether its function depends on where it is located. To test this, we use a system in the model organism C. elegans that allows us to artificially move dynein to a specific region, the spindle poles. We found that relocating dynein to the poles caused noticeable defects in cell division. In particular, cells showed misaligned chromosomes and failures in a key step called polar body extrusion. We also performed an embryonic lethality assay to assess the downstream effects of these defects and found significantly reduced embryo viability following dynein relocalization. Our findings suggest that dynein plays different roles depending on its position within the cell, and that disrupting its normal location interferes with proper cell division. By better understanding how proteins like dynein function in egg cells, this research may provide insight into the causes of chromosomal abnormalities and reproductive challenges.

title: "A snack is not a meal": Culture, Identity, and Dietary Change in Malawi
abstract: From KFC outlets in cities to freshly-fried potatoes in rural markets, Malawians have ever-increasing access to Westernized food options. Dominant frameworks for understanding dietary change predict an inevitable shift toward processed, unhealthy diets driven by income growth and urbanization. Without accounting for cultural nuances, however, such frameworks fail to capture uneven adoption of non-traditional ways of eating. Drawing on qualitative interviews, informal survey data and a historical analysis of Malawian food systems, this thesis proposes a four-part framework for understanding the social, cultural, and psychological dimensions through which Malawians navigate new food choices: financial pragmatism, competing heuristics of health and hygiene, the tension between tradition and novelty, and the weight of social perception. Central to this argument is the finding that a culturally specific distinction between a "snack" and a "real meal" functions as a mechanism of cultural appropriation, allowing Malawians to integrate Western food into their lives while maintaining a linguistic and conceptual separation from traditional eating habits. Furthermore, interviews reveal hygiene concerns are circumvented through brand-name heuristics and community-built online approval; health knowledge does not straightforwardly determine behavior; and status functions as an external enforcement mechanism which, unlike tradition, does not uniformly push against Western food but cuts in contradictory directions depending on context, generation, and the type of food involved. Together, these findings challenge homogenization narratives and call for food policy that engages not only with nutritional and economic dimensions, but with the cultural logic of eating.

title: Women Between Worlds: American Wives as Cultural Ambassadors in Meiji Japan
abstract: This research examines the role of American women in Meiji Japan as participants in cross-cultural exchange during a period of rapid political and social transformation. The research takes the form of a history thesis focused on Emma Wigmore, Mary Crawford Fraser, and Mary McNeill Fenollosa, who all traveled to Japan as the wives of foreign diplomats and hired professionals. It argues that expatriate wives functioned as informal, two-way cultural ambassadors who mediated between Japanese and American societies. Drawing on letters, diaries, and published writings as the primary source materials, this study foregrounds the experiences of three women to show how they interpreted Japanese culture for audiences at home while simultaneously introducing Euro-American customs into the spaces they occupied in Japan. The thesis situates these experiences within the broader context of Japan's efforts to renegotiate unequal treaties and assert its status as a modern nation in the late nineteenth century. As foreign diplomats, educators, and technical experts established communities in cities such as Yokohama and Tokyo, women became embedded in the social and domestic networks that sustained cross-cultural interaction in Japan. They engaged with Japanese people and culture by hosting gatherings, forming friendships, traveling, collecting material goods, and writing. This thesis demonstrates that by the end of the 1890s, these women were actively immersing themselves in Japanese society and producing knowledge about the country through published writings. This study expands the scope of diplomatic history during the Meiji Period and underscores the importance of women's experiences during this era.

title: Unleashed Horror in the Television: Examining Misrepresentations of the Insanity Plea in Contemporary Film and Television
abstract: Existing scholarship establishes that erroneous portrayals of the defense in widely disseminated film and television misconstrues audiences' understanding of its legal reality. The crucial gap, however, is that scholars do not address how such misrepresentations manifest in contemporary film and television. By close reading Primal Fear (1996), The Practice (2003), and CSI: Crime Scene Investigation (2011), this project aims to answer the following questions: (1) how does contemporary film and television perpetuate misconceptions of the insanity plea, and (2) how do such misrepresentations alter public perceptions of the legitimacy of the insanity plea? I found that the selected films and series, through visual and semantic representations, reflect three paradigmatic misconceptions of the insanity plea. My project locates instances where contemporary film and television misrepresent the insanity plea, ultimately contributing to broader scholarly conversations on the role of film and television in perpetuating misunderstandings of the law.

title: From the Atlantic to the Lakeshore: Practicing Samba and Constructing Brasilidade in Chicago
abstract: This sociological study explores how samba practitioners in Chicago teach, discuss, and perform samba as an Afro-Brazilian music and dance practice, and how this relates to race, nationalism, and identity in Brazil. While there is extensive scholarship on samba in Brazil, there is much less on samba outside Brazil, and in U.S. Latine studies and immigration studies Brazilians are understudied. There are a few older studies on one Chicago samba group but none on the current small, passionate, and interconnected scene. Motivated by my experiences attending Chicago samba events and interest in racialization, diaspora, and music related to Latin Americans in the U.S., including Brazilians, this study relies on semi-structured interviews with samba teachers and leaders from 7 organizations, as well as participant observations of samba classes and events. A transnational approach ties the data's emergent themes to ethnographies on samba in Brazil, as well as postcolonial and Movimento Negro scholarship. This study is ongoing, but early analysis indicates that a few key Afro-Brazilian leaders trained the majority of Chicago's samba dance teachers, resulting in a number of programs that forefront Afro-Brazilian history in their pedagogy, with some exceptions. They recruit new participants, primarily non-Brazilian and some Brazilians, through appeals to broad interest in Latin dance and festivities. To varying extents, samba organizations in Chicago perform samba as a form of Black diasporic resistance Chicagoans can join or learn about, as familiar national culture Brazilian immigrants can reconnect with, or as spectacle non-Brazilians can consume.

title: Storytelling & Video Editing for Protest Tradition: The NBA Bubble Podcast
abstract: In the summer of 2020, the NBA created a biosecure "bubble" at Disney World to finish its season amidst a global pandemic. Though often glazed over as a health, athletic, and financial success, this project examines the bubble's reckoning with the pandemic and the Black Lives Matter movement to reevaluate the practice of protest in sports. Drawing on news coverage, athlete statements, social media, and academic scholarship on race and sports media, this podcast investigates three questions: whether the bubble's geographic and economic isolation amplified or constrained political action; whether the two-day work stoppage constituted genuine protest or institutional management of dissent; and whether the negotiated outcome, expanded voting access, represented a meaningful resolution or a deflection from the core demand of ending police violence. The podcast further examines the tension between athletes' economic privilege and their inextricable Blackness, asking whether proximity to wealth severs or deepens connections within communities most harmed by racial violence. Our contributions included reviewing, selecting, and sequencing footage and audio; annotating raw footage; editing video clips using Premiere Pro and Descript; eliminating redundancies; creating promotional short-form content; and balancing humor and tragedy to shape an impactful narrative arc. Effort was dedicated to making the content accessible for all listeners to amplify the impact of sports' role in politics and calls for justice. This podcast asks who controlled the bubble, and to what end, challenging listeners to reflect on their own social values, expectations of athletes, and the opportunities for progress spurred by protest in sports.

title: Using Bio-compatible Conductive Hydrogels for On-Demand Drug Delivery
abstract: Liposomes, which are tiny spherical capsules made of the same material as cell membranes, have emerged as a promising platform for delivering chemotherapy drugs directly to solid tumors like breast and ovarian cancers. By encapsulating the drugs in these biocompatible spheres, researchers have made progress in protecting them from rapid clearance in the blood, something that has long limited the effectiveness of cancer treatments. However, the drugs are still cleared away from the tumor site too quickly to provide localized, long-lasting delivery. Hydrogels, which are water-swollen polymer networks similar in texture to soft tissue, offer a promising next step as encapsulated drugs are released slowly as the hydrogel is broken down by the body. Since the drug release rate depends on the mechanical properties of the hydrogel it is difficult to optimize. Our proposed solution to this issue involves creating conductive hydrogels that could release the encapsulated drugs on demand when an electrical signal is applied. This would allow for adaptive drug delivery, optimized to the patient's needs. To build this platform, we incorporated a conductive polymer called S-PEDOT into a sodium alginate hydrogel. We have already confirmed that our hydrogels have mechanical properties comparable to biological tissue and identified an optimal polymer composition that maximizes conductivity.
