The next step is loading these gels with drug-filled liposomes and demonstrating voltage-triggered release. This platform, which has not been previously reported in the literature, could ultimately enable precise, on-demand delivery of cancer drugs directly to solid tumor sites.

title: Foreclosure to Financialization: Mapping Institutional Investor Penetration in Single-Family Housing Markets After 2008
abstract: For many aspiring first-time homebuyers, the single-family home has shifted from a pathway to stability to a restricted financial asset, shaped in part by the post-2008 rise of institutional investors in the single-family rental market. This project examines how large-scale investor ownership has reshaped homeownership access, investigating whether it reflects a structural shift or a cyclical response to post-crisis conditions. Drawing on CoreLogic property-level data, the study constructs a longitudinal spatial dataset across three metropolitan areas [Atlanta, Charlotte, and Jacksonville] using kernel density estimation, spatial autocorrelation analysis, and demographic overlays to trace changes from a pre-investor baseline (2009) through a pre-COVID snapshot (2019) to the present (2025). Findings indicate statistically significant spatial clustering in Atlanta (Global Moran's I = 0.57, p < 0.001) and Charlotte (I = 0.32, p < 0.001), with Charlotte's clustering nearly doubling between 2019 and 2025. In Atlanta, 18 census tracts remained investor hotspots across both years. In Charlotte, high-investor tracts have median incomes 48% lower and Black population shares five times greater than low-investor tracts, consistent with investor targeting of historically distressed, minority-majority neighborhoods. Together, these patterns suggest institutional investor activity represents a durable structural transformation rather than a temporary crisis response. By mapping institutional portfolio intersections with historically accessible ownership opportunities, this project contributes to debates about financialization, intergenerational wealth-building, and housing equity. The evidence suggests institutional investors have reshaped the single-family market by concentrating ownership in distressed communities, reducing first-time buyer access to homeownership.

title: Mapping Movement Circuits: Projection-Specific Connectivity of Npas1+ Neurons in the Globus Pallidus Externa
abstract: The globus pallidus externa (GPe) is a region of the basal ganglia that regulates movement through genetically diverse neuron populations. Traditional models of basal ganglia circuitry treat the GPe as a relay within the indirect pathway through the subthalamic nucleus (STN), often overlooking the diversity of GPe neuron subtypes and their broader projection targets. However, emerging evidence has identified distinct GPe neuron populations based on molecular identity, axonal targets, and behavioral impacts, suggesting that the GPe's contributions to motor control extends beyond a single relay pathway. Among GPe neurons, Npas1+ cells constitute approximately 30% of the population and extend projections beyond classical basal ganglia pathways. Despite this, the organization and downstream targeting across motor-related brain regions remain poorly characterized. We hypothesized that Npas1+ GPe neurons form a distributed projection network with target-specific connectivity that modulates precise motor and action selection circuits. To test this, we used an intersectional genetic approach in Npas1-Flp;Ai14 mice combined with viral tracing to monosynaptically label neurons that receive Npas1+ GPe input. This cell-type specific strategy enabled identification of downstream targets through histological analysis. We observed projections to multiple motor-related regions, including the dorsal striatum, cortex, GPi, substantia nigra (pars reticulata and compacta), subthalamic nucleus, pedunculopontine nucleus, and olivary nuclei. Together, these findings demonstrate that Npas1+ GPe neurons participate in a distributed network rather than a single STN-mediated pathway, refining models of basal ganglia function and providing insight into how disruptions in GPe connectivity contribute to motor dysfunction in disorders such as Parkinson's disease.

title: @DarkHumor: Race-Blindness, Racism, and Racialization in Mexican Digital Discourse
abstract: The ideology of mestizaje, which touts the development of an exceptional “raceless” race through centuries of racial mixture in Latin America, is a core component of the Mexican identity. However, racism remains a central facet of Mexico’s landscape, perpetuating the erasure and subjugation of the Black, Indigenous, and Asian presence and experiences in the country’s national identity. Despite claiming unity, mestizaje sustains the race-blind conditions needed to ignore, deny, and disavow racism in Mexico. The public nature of social media can provide important insights into the process of racialization by providing an accessible view of popular reactions to racism. Digital satirical environments are rife with racist language, made permissible under the guise of dark humor. The novelty of digital social network research, coupled with the recency of the 2024 presidential elections, signal an opportunity to address understudied phenomena. I focus on a racist political post by popular Mexican meme account @EsDeMamador on X (previously Twitter) on the day of the election. I utilize an intersectional framework to analyze an array of 56 pre-selected (sub)replies to the original post. Drawing from literature on ethics in the digital humanities, Critical and Computer-Mediated Discourse Analysis, post-colonialism, and Critical Race Theory, I illuminate how non-racial categories (i.e., class, political party, religion) are weaponized as instruments of racialization. These reflect, refract, and advance exclusionary national imaginaries. My findings accentuate how white supremacy, anti-Blackness, and anti-Indigeneity continue to permeate daily interactions in Mexico today, despite the country’s alignment with race-blind ideologies.

title: A Deep Learning-Based Segmentation Model for Epithelial Cells Infected with Listeria monocytogenes
abstract: Accurate detection of objects from microscopy images, otherwise known as segmentation, is a necessary and limiting first step in quantifying cellular responses. In recent years, this process has been automated using tools such as Cellpose, which rely on neural networks trained on images with cytoplasmic or whole-cell fluorescence signal to segment cell borders. However, in multiplexed imaging approaches, this is challenging as there may not be enough channels to dedicate to segmentation. My project aims to evaluate whether I could use the biosensor signals, which vary between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, to develop a model to identify the borders of epithelial cells infected with the bacterial pathogen Listeria monocytogenes. To do this, I developed a computational pipeline to integrate the generalized segmentation model Cellpose-SAM with biosensor images from infected cells. As expected, basic Cellpose models were found to be unable to identify the borders of epithelial cells, preferring to segment the nucleus. I trained a model on manually annotated biosensor images and evaluated it using a standard metric, Intersection over Union. The trained model was able to identify the varied cytoplasmic signals from the biosensors, allowing for better segmentation of epithelial cell borders. To evaluate the utility of the model, I compared the results with those obtained using the Voronoi diagram, a commonly employed method for identifying cell borders in an epithelium. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of utilizing deep learning models for the segmentation of biosensor data, the identification of infected cells, and the quantification of bacterial load.

title: Experiences of Racial Mismatch and Relationship to Racial Belonging
abstract: The U.S. public school student body is projected to racially diversify over time, but these diverse students will be met with a rather homogenous teaching staff. Since 2011, the share of each racial and ethnic group in the public-school teaching force has not changed by more than 2 percentage points with 80% of teachers identifying as White. Research has identified the important role that teachers play in the lives of students, but scholars have lacked in the examination of how students of color experience their education led by mainly White teachers. With adolescence being an important life stage for racial and ethnic identity development, it is imperative that we understand the potential role that racial dynamics may play in identity development, specifically on racial, ethnic, and cultural belonging. The current research aimed to investigate how college students of color describe their experience with white teachers in high school and how, if at all, they describe the relationship between the experience of racial mismatch and their racial belonging. A sample of ten Northwestern first-year students of color participated in one-hour long interviews where they answered questions regarding their racial and ethnic identity, public school experience, and student-teacher relationship. Emerging findings demonstrate that participants did not articulate a White teacher's race as playing a role in their racial belonging, but many participants were able to express a desire for a teacher of color. This suggests the importance of diversifying the teaching field to fulfill students' desire of culturally connecting to their educators.

title: Modeling and Balance of Signed Directed Social Networks
abstract: My project looks at balance in directed, signed social networks. In a signed, directed network, connections between nodes can go either direction and can be positive or negative. In the context of this project, nodes are people, and connections can be measures of friendship or enmity. My research uses five datasets. As an example, one dataset is from Pardus, a video game where users can mark each other as friends or enemies (these need not be reciprocated). My project develops better randomization methods to better understand the structure of such networks by creating definitions of balanced triangles, meaning determining whether a given a set of three nodes and their connections is balanced. Some of the current literature suggests status theory as a possible definition of balance. We argue status theory has difficulty accounting for reciprocated and conflicting relationships (in the context of a trust network, reciprocated means both trust/distrust each other. Conflicting means trust one way but distrust the other). To test a new theory of balance, my project uses a randomized version of each network. To randomize the network my project uses a fixed topology randomization using a framework based on the maximum entropy principle. The number of nodes is the same and the edges are between the same nodes, and only the sign is randomized. This process only changes a very small number of the edges and preserves key aspects of the original network. We find the data is well aligned with two proposed definitions of balance.

title: A Pattern Emerges: Investigating Snail Family Transcription Factors' Role in Ectodermal Gene Regulation Networks
abstract: A crucial step in embryonic development is the specification of ectodermal cells into the three fates of the neural crest (NC), central nervous system (CNS) and skin (epidermis). The NC forms the peripheral nervous system & craniofacial skeleton and develops between the CNS and epidermis. These fates are separated into regions with defined boundaries, but disruptions can cause severe developmental defects. A complex regulatory network controls this specification but is incompletely understood; Snail family transcription factors (Snai 1/2) are good candidates for investigation of specification, as they regulate NC expression patterns at certain stages. This study investigated the hypothesis that Snail factors regulate gene expression during ectodermal fate determination to separate the three initially overlapping regions. Using Xenopus laevis embryos, Snail activity was manipulated through knockdown and overexpression approaches through injections of dominant-negative constructs and Snai1/2 mRNA respectively. Microinjections were conducted at the two-cell stage to target one side of the embryo, maintaining the other as an internal control. In situ hybridization probes targeted fate-specific marker genes foxd3 (NC), sox2/3 (CNS), and epik (epidermis) to visualize their expression and compare changes in expression patterns caused by the manipulations. epik results were inconsistent but informed later methods. Together, NC and CNS results indicated that Snail transcription factors define boundaries between the ectodermal fates by regulating genetic expression to simultaneously reduce specification into CNS and promote specification into NC. Ongoing work builds off these results, exploring how Snail factors regulate specification of cells directly in the boundaries between ectodermal fates.

title: Modeling Histone Chaperone Interactions at the Replication Fork to Elucidate Mechanisms of Genomic Stability
abstract: The diploid human genome comprises over 6 billion base pairs, totaling over 2 meters of DNA, that must be compacted to fit within the cell nucleus. To do this, DNA is wrapped around proteins called histones, forming chromatin, which must be transiently disassembled to allow the replication machinery access to the DNA, and subsequently reassembled to preserve genome stability. Histone chaperone proteins facilitate this process by escorting histones to correct locations during DNA replication and chromatin reorganization. These chaperones operate in a dynamic network with other chaperones and proteins at the replication fork. However, due to the complexity of this process, few physical interactions within this network have been found. This project aims to identify novel interactions among histone chaperones and replication fork proteins using computational structural modeling. We are employing the AlphaFold3.0 AI-based protein structure prediction tool on Northwestern University's QUEST high-performance computing system to generate high-confidence 3D protein complex structures. Models are assessed using the interface predicted template modeling (ipTM) score and a sliding-window assay to evaluate interaction stability. Highly confident predictions will be further analyzed using the PROtein binDIng enerGY (PRODIGY) analysis tool. Ultimately, predicted structures will be validated by coimmunoprecipitation in HEK293T cells and protein-binding assays with recombinant proteins. This ongoing work is expected to identify previously uncharacterized interactions within the histone chaperone network. These findings would provide a better understanding of how histones are relocated during DNA replication, offering insight into mechanisms underlying genome instability in certain diseases, such as cancer.

title: Evaluation of Heavy Metal Contamination and Social Correlates in Chicago Community Areas
abstract: Heavy metals are high-density elements that pose a significant toxicity risk to humans at elevated concentrations. Although naturally present in soil at low levels, human activity has contributed to heavy metal accumulation in urban areas, often disproportionately targeting marginalized communities. Since the level of heavy metal contamination in Chicago requires further exploration to improve evaluations of public health, this project aimed to quantify heavy metal contamination across Chicago's 77 community areas and assess its relationship with socioeconomic and racial demographics. We employed community-based methods to comprehensively survey areas of high human engagement with soil, such as playgrounds, and obtained soil samples from 60 community areas. Concentrations of heavy metals were quantified with Inductively Coupled Plasma-Optical Emission Spectroscopy. Using R and ArcGIS software, these results were geospatially integrated with demographic data from the U.S. Census Bureau and heavy metal regulations from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Holistically, our findings suggested that lower-income and majority non-white Chicago neighborhoods have higher concentrations of heavy metal contamination. Notably, community areas, such as Garfield Park and Brighton Park, consistently exhibited contamination levels that violated EPA thresholds for the majority of metals that were analyzed. Some heavy metals, including arsenic and chromium, exceeded EPA limits across all sampled locations. By elucidating heavy metal contamination patterns, our research highlights communities that are at risk and better informs future environmental policy decisions. Importantly, we emphasized collaborating with communities rather than acting as outside experts, which allows our work to empower communities and support local residents.

title: The Costs and Burden of In-Person Follow-Up After Pediatric Appendectomy
abstract: Appendectomy for uncomplicated appendicitis is the most common emergent surgery in pediatric patients, with roughly 70,000 annual cases nationally. Postoperative care typically includes an in-person follow-up visit, though telemedicine alternatives are being actively explored. The travel-related burdens of this practice remain poorly characterized. We retrospectively evaluated patients who underwent uncomplicated appendectomy at a single institution in 2020 to quantify time, cost, and environmental impacts of in-person follow-up. Patient zip codes were mapped to population-weighted centroids to estimate round-trip driving time and distance. Vehicle operating costs and carbon emissions were calculated from driving data using established national averages. Wage loss for one caregiver was calculated using the average Chicago metropolitan area wage and total time burden, which included a 30-minute allowance for parking, check-in, and waiting. Costs were inflation-adjusted to 2026 US dollars. Among 302 children undergoing uncomplicated appendectomy, the median round-trip drive time for in-person follow-up was 36.3 minutes (IQR 29.5–73.2), and the median estimated wage loss per family was $40.42 (IQR $36.27–$62.91). In aggregate, follow-up visits were associated with 273 total hours of driving and 9,899 miles driven, resulting in an estimated $7,176 in vehicle operating costs and $15,504 in wage loss. Carbon emissions attributable to driving totaled 3,519 kg CO2. In-person follow-up after uncomplicated pediatric appendectomy imposes substantial time, financial, and environmental burdens without proven clinical benefit. These findings underscore the need for comparative effectiveness research evaluating telemedicine-based vs. in-person postoperative follow-up strategies.

title: Theatre as Refuge: Facilitating Identity, Agency, and Belonging through Youth Migration Narratives at C:NTACT and Albany Park Theater Project
abstract: While migration research has addressed trauma, policy, and cultural integration, there remains a critical gap in understanding how the arts-theatre, in particular-can support migrant youth in navigating identity and belonging. Theatre offers unique affordances: it is embodied, collaborative, and rooted in storytelling, allowing young people to develop a sense of self and share narratives on their own terms. My thesis examines the pedagogical work of two youth theatre companies-C:NTACT in Copenhagen and Albany Park Theater Project in Chicago-to answer the following question: how do their devising processes employ identity-based theatre-making techniques to cultivate personal agency and social belonging among marginalized migrant youth, and what elements of these practices can be sustainably adapted to support refugee youth across diverse sociopolitical environments? Negotiations between individual and collective storytelling, institutional sustainability, and methods of audience engagement emerge as sites of key pedagogical insights-which are then applied to a preliminary model for the use of artistic techniques in refugee education spaces.

title: Investigating the Role of CARHSP1 in Stress Granule Formation and Metabolic Energy Production in Astrocytes
abstract: The brain often shows signs of stress before neurodegenerative diseases develop. My project explores how cells in the brain that directly support neurons, called astrocytes, respond to that stress and help protect neurons, particularly in conditions like dementia with Lewy bodies. While harmful protein aggregates are commonly linked to these diseases, growing evidence suggests the real issue may be a breakdown in how cells manage energy and internal balance. I am currently investigating the role of a protein called CARHSP1 in helping astrocytes respond to stress by producing energy for nearby neurons. To do this, I study cells grown under different nutrient conditions and modify CARHSP1 to observe how it affects two key processes: the formation of "stress granules," which store genetic instructions during stress, and the production of lactate, an important energy source. I also analyze which of the cell's genetic materials are stored during stress and test these findings in brain cells from mice. Finally, I simulate stress signals to see how astrocytes respond in real time. I expect to find that CARHSP1 plays an important role in regulating how astrocytes manage energy during stress. Understanding this process could reveal new ways to support brain cells and slow the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, offering insight into potential future treatments.

title: Misdiagnosis and Overdiagnosis of Learning and Behavioral Disorders in Black Students
abstract: Students across America with a variety of behavioral and learning disorders are able to succeed academically, socially, and professionally in their adult lives. Accurate diagnoses, treatment plans, and support from teachers and psychologists is crucial to a student's progression. However, there is a significant gap in accurate diagnostic and treatment services between Black students and White students in the Kindergarten-12th grade school system. Black students are often misdiagnosed or overdiagnosed with learning and behavioral disorders, therefore, holding them back from reaching their true academic potential. Examining how cultural biases embedded within Western general psychology have contributed to the inequitable diagnosis and treatment of Black students is essential for understanding the disparities they face in the American educational system. Moreover, this paper will adopt a cultural psychology approach to explore the underlying factors driving the overdiagnosis and misdiagnosis of Black students.

title: A Deep Learning Approach to Minimum Medial and Lateral Joint Space Width Measurement
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common joint disease worldwide and is characterized by progressive cartilage loss and joint space narrowing (JSN). Minimum joint space width (mJSW), the distance between femur and tibia, is a key radiographic indicator of OA progression and is central to diagnostic tools such as the Kellgren-Lawrence grading scale. However, JSW measurement is traditionally performed manually, making it time-consuming, observer-dependent, and impractical for large-scale studies or routine clinical use. This project presents a deep learning-based tool for objective, automated mJSW measurement from knee radiographs. The pipeline consists of a 5-class 2D UNet segmentation model trained to recognize medial and lateral compartments of bilateral posterior-anterior (PA) knee radiographs. Post-processing software measures the average vertical distance between the medial and lateral condyles using the predicted segmentation masks. Using these measurements and metadata, mJSW is calculated in millimeters. Testing and training sets were sourced from the OAI dataset (125 and 300 images). Comparison of the segmentation model against a validation set revealed congruency between predicted and annotated masks, with agreement exceeding 87% across all classes. Evaluation on a 100-image set showed that 92% of predictions were within 1mm of manual measurements. The average mJSW across the test set, when stratified by OARSI JSN grade, demonstrated a strong inverse correlation (r=-0.91). This model shows significant potential in accurately predicting mJSW. This would be of marked benefit to clinicians. Future work will refine the model and explore its ability to capture trends across Kellgren-Lawrence grades.

title: Platelets drive immune suppression and glioblastoma growth in a sex-dependent manner via PAR4 signaling
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common primary malignant brain tumor, with outcomes shaped by biological sex differences that influence disease progression, immune function, and interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Although platelets are increasingly recognized as active participants in tumor biology, their contribution to sex-specific immune regulation in GBM has not yet been defined. We identify platelet PAR4 signaling as a central mechanism linking sex hormones to antitumor immunity. To investigate the role of platelets in the immunosuppressive TME, we investigated human platelet function, genetic and pharmacologic perturbation of PAR4, hormone manipulation, and immune profiling of tumor-infiltrating cells. We found that GBM patients display elevated platelet activation driven by protease-activated receptor 4 (PAR4). In vivo, inhibition of PAR4 extended survival in females but not males, and we have shown this benefit is estrogen dependent.. Mechanistically, PAR4 inhibition increases CD8+ T-cell infiltration into the TME, establishing a platelet-driven, sex specific immune response. We further show that estrogen receptor v physically interacts with PAR4 to amplify calcium signaling in platelets, revealing a previously unrecognized hormone-receptor crosstalk that shapes platelet behavior in tumors. PAR4-activated platelets suppress CD8+ T-cell function within the TME, and depletion of CD8+ T cells eliminates both the heightened platelet reactivity induced by GBM and the survival advantage conferred by PAR4 inhibition. Together, these findings identify platelet PAR4 signaling as a regulator of GBM progression and reveal sex-dependent immune mechanisms as critical determinants of therapeutic response and offering therapeutic targets for sex-dependent GBM treatment.

title: Performing Equity, Missing Change: Exploring Teacher Perspectives on "Accountability Theater" in a Diverse Suburban High School
abstract: Faced with pressures from the local school board and state laws to reduce racial disparities in student discipline, Franklin High sought to improve both its discipline metrics and student-realized outcomes. However, only the former was meaningfully addressed. This study examines how the school engaged in "accountability theater," defined as performative compliance that satisfies external demands without producing substantive change. Although these policies were intended to promote equity, they often backfired when teachers interpreted them as superficial or disconnected from classroom realities. For example, teachers were told to stop writing referrals without clear disciplinary alternatives, leaving them feeling unsupported and uncertain about how to manage their classrooms. As a result, teachers either reluctantly complied with administrative directives or ignored them. This study asks: When and how did teachers recognize the accountability pressures facing Franklin High? How did their perceptions of the school's initiatives shape trust in leadership and colleagues? Did teachers observe meaningful improvements for students? Drawing on ethnographic interviews with 44 teachers from 2019 to 2024, three main findings emerge. First, teachers varied in awareness of the external pressures driving these changes. Second, most teachers agreed racial disparities in discipline were a real and important issue, driving a want for change and an observed lack of improvement. Third, many viewed administrative responses as disconnected from classroom realities, leading to diminished trust in leadership. Accountability efforts must align with the day-to-day realities teachers face in their classrooms in order to enact lasting change for students, schools, and communities.

title: Extension of DNA Dendrimers through the Hybridization Chain Reaction
abstract: Cancerous tumors suppress the immune system, making it harder for the body to fight them and kill cancer cells. One promising approach to reverse this is by activating the cGAS-STING pathway. This pathway triggers an immune response when a protein called cGAS detects foreign DNA inside a cell, allowing immune cells to kill cancer cells. Longer DNA activates this more effectively, but getting DNA into cells is difficult. DNA dendrimers, branched, tree-like molecules, have been shown to improve the delivery of DNA into cells at once. However, making dendrimers with branches long enough to reliably trigger the immune alarm is difficult, as demonstrated by low yields. This study explored a solution using a process called the hybridization chain reaction (HCR). HCR is like a molecular chain reaction where a short "starter" piece of DNA (Initiator DNA) causes two coiled DNA molecules to unfold and link together repeatedly, producing long DNA chains. Two strategies for combining HCR with DNA dendrimers were tested. The first, building dendrimers from one of the coiled DNA components, proved synthetically impossible due to the complexity of those components. The second strategy, attaching the short, simple Initiator DNA to the dendrimer, produced the desired dendrimer with an acceptable 11% yield. We confirmed that dendrimers carrying multiple starters produced significantly longer DNA chains than Initiator DNA alone. This demonstrates that DNA dendrimers can drive the chain reaction more powerfully than linear DNA, enabling the creation of larger immune-activating DNA structures than was previously possible.

title: "It's Okay Sometimes": Insights into Students' Nuanced Evaluations of Their Programming Ability While Using LLMs
abstract: Amid concerns that computer science students are over-relying on large language models (LLMs), this paper seeks to explore how students perceive and assess their programming ability while coding with an LLM. Student self-assessments of their programming ability can help us understand how students experience learning, providing insight into how we can support the development of introductory instruction that integrates LLMs while fostering student confidence, learning, and self-efficacy. We conducted two survey studies, totaling 52 participants, to investigate how students assess programming ability while coding with an LLM. Our first (qualitative) survey allowed us to identify a set of moments during which students may evaluate programming ability while coding with an LLM, such as checking code correctness with an LLM. Our second (quantitative) survey investigated how students self-assessed their own abilities when they encountered these newly-defined moments as well as moments identified in prior research before LLMs were widely accessible. Our findings revealed parallels between student self-assessment data gathered prior to and after the introduction of LLMs. They also indicated that students think critically about LLM usage while programming. We ask whether student self-assessments based on our newly defined moments are accurate judgements of their programming ability and whether the accuracy of these judgments varies depending on student interests and goals. We call on researchers and practitioners to question what programming skills and LLM use cases suit the interests and needs of their students and to encourage the development of those skills and behaviors as a means of supporting student self-efficacy.

title: An Uncertain Peace: Armed Groups, Civilian Disputes, and the Limits of State Presence in Postwar Colombia
abstract: Colombia's 2016 Peace Accords, signed between the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and the Colombian government, ended the Western Hemisphere's longest civil war. However, uncertainty remains about the continued presence of armed groups and whether civilians turn to the state or other actors to resolve disputes. Scholarship on Colombian postwar governance often focuses on top-down provision of goods rather than bottom-up civilian experiences. This study draws on survey and interview data collected across 20 Colombian municipalities and roughly 60 communities, using regression analysis to identify patterns in dispute resolution behavior and thematic analysis of interviews to explain these patterns. In locations where armed groups remained after the 2016 Accords, residents were three times more likely to say they "don't know" whether they would use state mechanisms to resolve disputes than those in communities without armed group presence. This finding suggests that the boundary between state and non-state authority has become unclear, leaving civilians unsure who to turn to for dispute resolution. In communities exposed to armed groups during the civil war, residents were 50-60% less likely to use state mechanisms today than those with no wartime armed group presence, reflecting distrust rooted in wartime experiences of state violence and abandonment. This research contributes to post-conflict governance debates by demonstrating that the presence of armed groups continues to fragment civilian engagement with state institutions. These findings reveal a gap in Colombia's 2016 Peace Accords, which left unresolved questions about armed group dynamics and civilian trust in the state.

title: Proteomimetic Polymer for Neuron-Targeted Delivery.
abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) play essential roles in cellular function and are implicated in many neurodegenerative disorders. In neurodegenerative diseases, some of these interactions go wrong, causing proteins to clump together in ways that damage and ultimately kill brain cells. One promising therapeutic strategy is using short protein fragments called peptides to selectively block these harmful interactions. However, peptides break down quickly in the body and have difficulty entering cells, which limits their usefulness as treatments. Protein-like polymers (PLPs) are an emerging class of materials that mimic peptides while overcoming these limitations. By linking many peptide units together onto a stable backbone, PLPs offer improved durability, multivalency, and better ability to enter cells compared to peptides alone. A major challenge in treating brain diseases is delivering therapeutics specifically affected cell types such as neurons. This project focused on the use of the Tet-1 peptide, a short sequence originally identified for its ability to bind neuronal receptors. We investigated the hypothesis that PLPs derived from the Tet-1 peptide sequence would retain their targeting ability while gaining the advantages of the polymer platform. Tet-1 based monomers were synthesized, assembled into polymers, and fluorescently labeled to track their localization into cells. The polymers were characterized to confirm their structure and consistency. Our results support Tet-1 derived PLPs for cellular targeting and internalization, establishing a promising platform for delivering future therapeutics to brain cells.

title: Exploring How Aggressive Immigration Policies and Anti-Immigrant Rhetoric Affect Latino Immigrant Health
abstract: Health disparities among Latine immigrants in the United States are shaped not only by individual behaviors but also by political rhetoric, public discourse, and immigration policy. This project examines how anti-immigrant rhetoric and aggressive immigration enforcement function as social determinants of health, producing physical and mental health consequences for Latine immigrant communities. Drawing on scholarship, this work situates contemporary anti-immigrant discourse within the long-standing "Latino Threat Narrative," which racializes Latine immigrants as criminal, threats, and culturally incompatible. Using the framework developed by Vargas, Sanchez, and Juarez, which links hostile anti-immigrant policy environments to adverse health outcomes, this project explores how rhetoric and policy are embodied through material, psychosocial, and behavioral pathways. These mechanisms include chronic stress, fear of detention and deportation, avoidance of healthcare and social services, unsafe working and housing conditions, and increased rates of anxiety, depression, and somatic symptoms. Notably, the effects extend beyond unauthorized immigrants to authorized individuals and mixed-status families, demonstrating how immigration enforcement produces widespread community-level harm. The project also highlights how language itself, through criminalizing labels and repeated narratives, contributes to health inequities by shaping lived experience and daily decision-making. By framing immigration policy as health policy, this work underscores the ethical and public health implications of anti-immigrant rhetoric. Ultimately, it argues for greater scholarly attention to immigrant health and for policy approaches grounded in human rights and health equity.

title: What's the junction's function? Quantifying molecular load of dynamic crosslinks in polymer networks.
abstract: Covalent adaptable networks (CANs) are an exciting class of polymeric materials capable of self-healing and reprocessing through topological network reconfiguration. They are an emerging alternative to thermosets, which are high-strength materials composed of polymer chains crosslinked by strong, irreversible bonds. Such bonds make thermosets difficult to recycle and thereby are single-time use. CANs aim to provide a solution to the high rates of plastic waste. However, for CANs to be a true alternative to thermosets, they must be able to withstand high levels of mechanical force during use and reprocessing. Despite decades of research, there is a limited understanding of the mechanical failure of CANs on a molecular level. This knowledge gap poses significant issue, as understanding on the molecular level is essential to design robust CANs suitable for the replacement of thermosets. Force-sensitive small molecules, known as mechanophores, undergo predictable chemical transformation upon critical stress. Through the incorporation of intentionally weak, mechanosensing bonds, damage within CANs can be quantified during and after failure of the material's structure, and self-healing can autonomously occur to restore the original properties. Current work in the Kalow lab quantifies the mechanical load of fully dynamic crosslinks within CANs, providing partial insight into the mechanism of mechanical failure. To investigate the load-bearing capabilities of the polymer backbone-crosslinker junction, mechanophore activation is measured via fluorescence within a hybrid static-dynamic crosslink. Greater understanding of this physical property will allow for application of CANs on a bulk scale, making CANs an increasingly accessible and sustainable alternative to thermosets.

title: Identifying Block Design Task Completion Strategies With Machine Learning
abstract: The Block Design Task (BDT) is a spatial intelligence task that requires participants to arrange colorful blocks into a target design, providing a unique opportunity to capture individual differences in spatial thinking. However, past studies on variations in how participants complete the BDT have relied on time-consuming manual video reviews. Machine learning (ML) refers to a category of computational tools to automatically detect patterns in data, which can accelerate analyses of complex behavioral data. This project assesses the viability of sensor-embedded blocks alongside ML methods for more efficient analyses of inter-participant strategic variations in completing the BDT. We collected data from 57 undergraduate students who each completed seven BDT target designs without time constraints. Embedded sensors indicated each block's relative position over time, providing information on each participant's block placement sequences. We developed a custom hierarchical time series clustering algorithm to quantify strategic similarities between participants and identify potential participant groupings. Preliminary results for one target design showed no discernible groupings, but the algorithm's judgments of similarities between participants aligned with qualitative video-based judgments. This suggests that the algorithm can effectively capture inter-participant patterns in BDT strategies regardless of whether underlying groupings exist. Further analyses will be conducted to assess the ML algorithm across the remaining target designs. If our methodology with sensor-embedded blocks and ML-based analyses consistently captures patterns between participants, similar approaches may help expedite and scale future research on how participants approach the BDT.

title: Combination Treatment of DFMO and Navitoclax for Medulloblastoma, a Childhood Brain Cancer
abstract: Medulloblastoma is a type of childhood brain cancer that arises in the part of the brain that controls coordination, balance, and other complex motor functions. It is the most common cancerous pediatric brain tumor, and the typical course of treatment includes surgical removal of the tumor, chemotherapy, and radiation. In cases of medulloblastoma relapse, there is a very low survival rate, which is why it is important to find curative treatment options. This research explores the effect of combining two drugs on medulloblastoma cancer cells. Difluoromethylornithine, or DFMO, is a drug that halts cell growth by inducing a state of “senescence” in cells. This is followed by a second drug, Navitoclax, which selectively eliminates these senescent cells. First, it was confirmed that DFMO induces senescence in medulloblastoma cells. To explore the combination effect of these two drugs, medulloblastoma cells were first treated with DFMO for 96 hours, followed by a range of concentrations of Navitoclax for 48 hours. The proportion of cancer cells that survived the treatment was measured, where a lower level of “viability” meant the treatment was more effective at eliminating the cancer cells. The sequential DFMO–Navitoclax treatment reduced the viability of medulloblastoma cancer cells to a greater extent than either drug alone, indicating that this combination may be an effective therapeutic approach.

title: Precision In Situ Measurement of Rotor Wobble in the ARIADNE Axion Experiment
abstract: Dark matter makes up most of the matter in the universe, yet its identity remains a mystery. The ARIADNE experiment at Northwestern will search for a promising dark matter candidate called the axion. To do this, the experiment utilizes a spinning tungsten rotor located extremely close, within 75 micrometers, of a sensitive quantum-based sensor. If the axion exists, it would produce a measurable signal we can detect using a magnetic measurement technique. A challenge of the experiment is the stability of the rotor. Small displacements or “wobble” of the rotor can lead to collisions with the detector, damaging the experiment. A reliable measurement method to track displacements of the rotor on the order of several micrometers is necessary. This system must be able to operate under extreme experimental conditions, including temperatures reaching -452 ºF and high vacuum pressures. We developed a method utilizing a fiber interferometer, a laser sent down an optical fiber, to track the wobble of the rotor with high precision. As the distance between the fiber and rotor changes, the signal we measure shifts in a predictable manner. By calibrating this relationship between the signal and distance, we can convert the signal into precise measurements of the rotor’s position within the experiment. Initial tests show that this method can track the wobble of the rotor with high precision, and we have characterized the wobble of the rotor measuring displacements of 20 micrometers. This technique will be utilized to ensure safe operation of the rotor within ARIADNE.

title: Language Matters; How Adults with Food Insecurity Perceive the Term "Binge Eating"
abstract: Nearly one fifth of Americans experience food insecurity, meaning they do not have consistent access to nutritious food. Food insecurity often leads to a cycle of food scarcity followed by overeating when food is available; this cycle can contribute to binge eating, a serious but often overlooked health concern. However, most binge eating research has focused on a narrow population (skinny, white, affluent, girls). Consequently, language used to describe binge eating may not resonate with individuals experiencing food insecurity. Therefore, we explored whether the term "binge eating" resonates with this population, and if alternative words like "emotional eating" or "overeating" better reflect their experiences. We conducted a thematic analysis from interview data with 26 adults with food insecurity who received a digital binge eating intervention. Participants described mixed reactions to the term "binge eating." Some felt it accurately described their experiences, while others found it too broad or stigmatizing. Several participants preferred the terms "emotional eating" or "uncontrolled eating" because they felt these better captured their experiences without implying a diagnosis. Some participants identified with "binge eating," but their personal definitions did not consistently match the clinical definition, indicating a misunderstanding. These findings suggest that current language around binge eating may not fully resonate with individuals experiencing food insecurity. When people do not see themselves reflected in terminology, they may be less likely to seek support or may view interventions as irrelevant. This highlights the need for more inclusive, accessible language in eating disorder research and intervention outreach.

title: Toward Autonomous Breathing: Predicting CO2 in Children with CCHS Using Wearable Sensors
abstract: Breathing is something that most people rarely think about, seamlessly adapting to changes in sleep, exercise, or everyday movement. But for children with Congenital Central Hypoventilation Syndrome (CCHS), this automatic control is impaired, requiring reliance on assisted ventilation to breathe. Advances such as phrenic nerve stimulation have enabled patients to live longer and more active lives by restoring diaphragm function. However, these systems still depend on manual, clinician-driven adjustments, limiting their ability to respond in real time to changing metabolic demands. This project investigates whether a patient's ventilatory needs can be anticipated before physiological signals reflect these changes. Transcutaneous CO2 (tcCO2), a key clinical measure of ventilation, is inherently delayed due to physiological and diffusion constraints, restricting its use in real-time control. To address this, we developed a predictive framework using noninvasive wearable signals. We built upon an existing sensing platform and designed an experimental protocol to capture interactions between ventilation and activity. Using synchronized expired CO2 (etCO2) and accelerometry data, we trained a machine learning model (CNN to biLSTM) to learn these physiological patterns. The model was able the identify the delay between signals and predict future CO2 levels with mean absolute errors of 0.55-0.58 mmHg. These results demonstrate the feasibility of predicting clinically meaningful CO2 dynamics from wearable data, providing a foundation for closed-loop, anticipatory control of phrenic nerve stimulation. Future work will focus on building a large, diverse physiological dataset across individuals, enabling personalized and adaptive respiratory support across age, activity level, and patient variability.

title: Impact of Myeloid-Specific MyD88 Deficiency on Inflammatory Cell Responses Following Lung Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury in Latent MCMV Infection
abstract: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) establishes lifelong latency in many individuals and poses significant risks to immunocompromised patients, especially organ transplant recipients. Lung ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) is a common consequence of transplantation and induces significant inflammation that can influence viral reactivation. Myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) is a key adaptor protein in innate immune signaling pathways and plays a key role in regulating inflammatory responses. Therefore, this study investigates the role of myeloid-specific MyD88 signaling in modulating innate immune responses during latent MCMV infection and lung IRI. To investigate this, a tamoxifen-inducible, myeloid-specific MyD88 knockout mouse model underwent lung IRI. Immune cell populations in lung tissue, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), and spleen were analyzed by flow cytometry. DNA was isolated from lung and salivary gland tissue and used in quantitative PCR (qPCR) to assess MCMV viral burden via immediate-early gene (IE-1) copy number. Preliminary flow cytometry data suggest differences in inflammatory cell populations, including neutrophils, CD11b+ cells, and interstitial macrophages between MyD88-deficient and control groups. qPCR analyses of MCMV IE-1 copy number across lung and salivary gland tissues are ongoing. Further analyses will characterize these immune and virologic trends and determine the extent to which MyD88 signaling influences the balance between inflammatory injury and viral control following lung IRI. These findings may provide insight into therapeutic targeting of inflammatory pathways in transplant settings.

title: Construction of the Deportable Body: The Ontology of "Reasonable Suspicion" and Noem V. Vasquez Perdomo
abstract: This thesis traces the genealogy of the reasonable suspicion legal standard and examines its contemporary application in Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo (2025). In Perdomo, Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh permitted race, language, occupation, and location to function as indicators of undocumented status. This thesis argues that Kavanaugh's interpretation of reasonable suspicion is a racialized project, disproportionately targeting Brown-skinned Latine individuals. Drawing on three foundational reasonable suspicion majority opinions alongside analysis of social media documentation of detainments, this thesis demonstrates how the ontology of reasonable suspicion has been reformulated to target Brown-skinned Latine individuals. I introduce the deportable body as a social construct to emphasize how Immigration Enforcement Officers automatically label Brown bodies as "illegal." By situating Perdomo within broader histories of racialization, this project ultimately reframes reasonable suspicion not as a neutral legal standard, but as a tool that produces non-belonging and institutionalizes racialized disposability in the United States.

title: Historical Knowledge: Development of Normative Data for Historical Misconceptions Study
abstract: People's beliefs about history reflect and shape future-oriented public policy. Some of these beliefs may be misinformed, particularly due to differential information uptake for historical topics. Construal level theory suggests that information about temporally distant, historical events may be recalled more abstractly as compared to information about proximal, contemporary events. Increased psychological distance encourages greater reliance on general, distinguishing features rather than on details. To study how historical information is reproduced, we developed a set of 64 conceptually-matched questions related to 32 unfamiliar distal (e.g., "What city did the Erie Canal make the primary seaport in the U.S. in the late 1800s?") and 32 unfamiliar proximal (e.g., "What port has been most impacted by the Trump administration's import tariffs?") U.S. historical events to be used in misinformation experiments. We normed these materials by asking 160 participants to answer each of the 64 open-ended questions, indicate their confidence in their responses, and rate their familiarity with the topics. Participants' response accuracy ranged from 1.32% to 87.50%. We identified and analyzed the 24 distal/proximal pairs with the lowest accuracy (30.76% average) for use in future studies. Correlational analyses indicated that response confidence was weakly correlated with accuracy (r = 0.32), familiarity with the question topic was moderately correlated with accuracy (r = 0.59), and familiarity was strongly correlated with confidence (r = 0.82). These normed materials will be used in planned experiments to examine the influence of psychological distance on readers' uptake of and reliance on inaccurate historical ideas.

title: Efficacy of Tomivosertib (MNK1/2 Inhibitor) in Mitigating Pain in a Mouse Model of Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa
abstract: Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (RDEB) is a rare genetic disease that causes extremely fragile skin, leading to frequent blistering, wounds, and scarring. In addition to visible skin damage, many patients experience chronic nerve-related pain, especially during routine care like changing bandages. Current treatments, such as morphine and gabapentin, often provide limited relief and can have significant side effects. In this study, we investigated whether a specific cellular pathway, called the MAP Interacting Protein Kinase (MNK) signaling pathway, contributes to this chronic pain. We used a mouse model of RDEB that closely mimics the human disease, including both skin symptoms and pain-related behaviors. We found that several genes involved in the MNK pathway were more active in pain-sensing nerves of RDEB mice compared to healthy controls, suggesting this pathway may be overactive in the disease. To test whether blocking this pathway could reduce pain, we treated RDEB mice with a drug called tomivosertib, which inhibits MNK signaling. Treated mice showed reduced activity of pain-related genes and exhibited fewer pain behaviors, such as excessive grooming and facial grimacing. These findings suggest that overactivation of the MNK pathway may play a key role in chronic pain in RDEB. Targeting this pathway with drugs like tomivosertib could offer a new and more effective approach for managing pain in patients with this condition.

title: All Cracked Up: How Solvents Stress Out Hydrogels
abstract: Poly(ethylene glycol)-based hydrogels are widely used in biomedical and soft robotic systems such as drug delivery and tissue engineering due to their ability to absorb solvents while maintaining their structural integrity and then revert back to their size. Here, we study drying, the dynamic process which occurs when solvent evaporates from a fully swollen gel. The drying process induces internal stress gradients that can lead to cracking, peeling, or fracturing, which limits practical applications for these materials. Here, we investigate drying-induced fracturing and peeling of PEG-based hydrogels, focusing on how solvent volatility, crosslinking density, and gel thickness influences these behaviors. We find that cracking and peeling behavior does not vary significantly across changes in gel thickness or crosslinker density, but it does depend on the volatility of the solvent. More volatile solvents lead to faster drying, as well as a greater extent of material fracturing. By quantifying the behaviors of drying-induced fractures, our research provides insights into these mechanics and offers strategies to design more durable PEG-based hydrogels. These insights also advance our understanding of solvent-gel interactions in various drying conditions and can be used to help inform the design of systems that rely on structural integrity and minimal instabilities.

title: Storytelling & Video Editing for Protest Tradition: The NBA Bubble Podcast
abstract: In the summer of 2020, the NBA created a biosecure "bubble" at Disney World to finish its season amidst a global pandemic. Though often glazed over as a health, athletic, and financial success, this project examines the bubble's reckoning with the pandemic and the Black Lives Matter movement to reevaluate the practice of protest in sports. Drawing on news coverage, athlete statements, social media, and academic scholarship on race and sports media, this podcast investigates three questions: whether the bubble's geographic and economic isolation amplified or constrained political action; whether the two-day work stoppage constituted genuine protest or institutional management of dissent; and whether the negotiated outcome, expanded voting access, represented a meaningful resolution or a deflection from the core demand of ending police violence. The podcast further examines the tension between athletes' economic privilege and their inextricable Blackness, asking whether proximity to wealth severs or deepens connections within communities most harmed by racial violence. Our contributions included reviewing, selecting, and sequencing footage and audio; annotating raw footage; editing video clips using Premiere Pro and Descript; eliminating redundancies; creating promotional short-form content; and balancing humor and tragedy to shape an impactful narrative arc. Effort was dedicated to making the content accessible for all listeners to amplify the impact of sports' role in politics and calls for justice. This podcast asks who controlled the bubble, and to what end, challenging listeners to reflect on their own social values, expectations of athletes, and the opportunities for progress spurred by protest in sports.

title: Engineering Galectin-mimicking Nanoparticles for Targeting Lung Cancer
abstract: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related mortality. Despite recent advances in immunotherapy, the clinical response rate for treatments remains below 50%. This warrants the development of targeted therapeutics and biomarker discovery for safe and effective delivery of these agents. Tumor-associated carbohydrate antigens (TACAs) are glycans overexpressed in cancer that contribute to a suppressive tumor microenvironment and represent promising targets. However, their potential remains underexplored due to heterogenous glycosylation. To address this gap, I developed a nanoparticle panel for systematic investigation of glycan-mediated tumor-immune interactions. In this work, I use nanoparticles displaying novel peptides derived from galectins, a class of carbohydrate-binding proteins that bind to β-galactose-containing glycans with varying affinity and specificity. Lectin staining confirmed the presence of β-galactose on human lung cancer cells (A549) which increased following sialidase treatment. Peptides derived from carbohydrate recognition domains (CRDs) of galectins were then conjugated to poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) nanoparticles which enables multivalent presentation and increased binding avidity. Fluorescence microscopy in A549 cells showed greater Galectin-3 nanoparticle (Gal3s-NP) binding per cell compared to the control (mean 2.17 vs 1.68, p=0.002). Flow cytometry further demonstrated increased Gal3s-NP binding in A549 relative to human T cells (1.92 vs 1.29-fold change over control). Thus, I found that galectin-mimicking nanoparticles enable increased specificity for cancer epithelial cells. I expect that our nanoparticle platform will shed insights into dissecting complex tumor-immune interactions with potential to improve targeted delivery of existing and emerging anticancer agents. Future work will expand to additional galectins and ex vivo tissues.

title: Examining the Relationship Between Musical Sophistication and Technologically Mediating Listening Experiences
abstract: With the introduction of all-access music streaming platforms, there has been a noticeable shift in user behavior as listeners move away from radio-broadcast systems toward a more individualized experience. Previous research has investigated how users interact with these platforms and found a correlation with musical sophistication, measured using the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Gold-MSI; Mullensiefen, et al. 2014), suggesting that listening behaviors can predict musical sophistication (Ferwerda & Graus, 2018). This study examines the relationship between listener types and musical sophistication using two psychometric instruments: the Streamed Listening Index of Musical Experience (SLIME) and the Gold-MSI. Data collection is still ongoing (anticipated n=300). These findings have implications for how we theorize the relationship between immersion in music and technologically mediated listening. A deeper understanding of the relationship between musical sophistication and a critical awareness of recommendation systems can help us to better understand the nature of intentional vs. passive consumption in music, which could contribute to our understanding of relationships between training and enculturation, implicit and explicit knowledge, and broader elements of musical absorption (cf. Sandstrom and Russo, 2013). Future work will examine whether this relationship holds across listener subgroups and how specific dimensions of sophistication - such as musical training, engagement, and perceptual abilities - differentially predict algorithmic awareness. Ultimately, this research aims to refine psychometric tools appropriate for studying music listening in algorithmically shaped environments.

title: Self similarity of Fractals
abstract: What does it mean to measure the complexity of a shape when it is too irregular to be described by notions like length or area? Fractals provide a compelling example: they are geometric sets in which similar patterns repeat at different scales, so that zooming in reveals smaller copies of the overall structure. Classic examples include the Cantor set and the Sierpinski gasket, which are constructed through iterative processes yet produce intricate forms. A key tool for quantifying this complexity is the Hausdorff dimension, which extends the idea of dimension beyond integers and captures how "dense" a set is at arbitrarily small scales. Unlike standard dimensions (such as 1 for a line or 2 for a surface), fractals often have non-integer values. This project investigates how Hausdorff dimension behaves under transformations. While some transformations preserve dimension, there is no simple general criterion for when it remains unchanged. To address this, I study classical fractals and apply transformations including scaling, nonlinear distortions, and projections, comparing their dimensions before and after transformation. The results reveal a sharp contrast. Transformations that preserve geometric structure, such as uniform scaling, also preserve Hausdorff dimension. In contrast, transformations that collapse structure, such as projecting a two-dimensional fractal onto a line, can reduce it. These findings show that fractal complexity is stable under some transformations but sensitive to others. This work highlights the dependence of fractal geometry on representation and points to the open problem of characterizing which transformations preserve Hausdorff dimension.

title: Food Difficulties Associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Travel Experiences
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is often associated with various food difficulties, including pickiness and sensory sensitivities, which often result in a reliance on familiar, preferred foods. These food sensitivities have been studied frequently in children, but there is little known about how food difficulties manifest for adults with autism. Even less is known about how food difficulties associated with ASD affect adults’ relationship to traveling and experience of a new place. The present study examined the relationship between travel and ASD-associated food difficulties in the form of an anonymous self-report questionnaire conducted via Qualtrics. The self-report questionnaire included the Swedish Eating Assessment for Autism Spectrum Disorders (SWEAA) to assess issues related to eating and mealtimes in adults with autism, in addition to behavioral and attitudinal questions aimed to more specifically investigate people’s travel experiences as related to food and eating, including but not limited to anxiety or stress around food selection when traveling. Food is an integral part of the travel experience, and traveling often disrupts familiar routines and limits access to preferred foods. Participants reported moderate levels of the following: food sensitivities, general preferences for familiar foods and mealtime routines, and food-related difficulties during travel. Studying these food difficulties can increase understanding about the stressors adults with autism may face when traveling, inform more inclusive travel planning, and lead to travel-targeted interventions and general public awareness surrounding complex experiences with food and travel. Future research should explore how to improve travel for adults with autism who experience food difficulties.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotide-Mediated Knockdown of ZFP423 in Adipose Tissue Enhances Thermogenesis and Improves Metabolic Health
abstract: Circadian rhythms are present among nearly all organisms on Earth and serve to predict the metabolic demands of the day. Disruption of circadian rhythms due to shiftwork, night-time eating, and interrupted sleep increases risk for diabetes and obesity. Recent studies demonstrated that circadian disruption through time-restricted feeding (TRF) during the inactive period disrupts thermogenesis, leading to greater risk of diabetes and obesity. Genetically knocking out zinc finger protein 423 (ZFP423), a gene that is normally responsible for maintaining white adipose tissue, promotes the formation of "beige" adipocytes and enhances thermogenesis. We recently found that knocking out ZFP423 prevents the negative effects of inactive period TRF. We hypothesized that a drug designed to knock down ZFP423 could make an effective therapy for diabetes and obesity, so we designed ZFP423-targeting Antisense Oligonucleotides (ASOs), an RNA-targeting therapeutic, modified to target adipose tissue. Following four weeks of weekly ASO injections, wild-type mice were given a glucose tolerance test and then placed into Sable metabolic phenotyping chambers to measure food intake, oxygen consumption, daily activity, respiratory exchange ratio, and energy expenditure. Lastly, we collected tissue samples from mice to perform qPCR on cDNA from these samples. We found that mice with ZFP423 knocked down exhibited improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, and reduced adiposity. The mice also showed increased oxygen consumption and energy expenditure without changes in activity. Together, this study indicates that ASO knockdown of ZFP423 enhances thermogenesis. These findings may help identify new therapies for combating obesity and metabolic disease.

title: Heavy Metal Contamination in Chicago
abstract: Heavy metals are high-density elements that pose a significant toxicity risk to humans at elevated concentrations. Although naturally present in soil at low levels, human activity has contributed to heavy metal accumulation in urban areas, often disproportionately targeting marginalized communities. Since the level of heavy metal contamination in Chicago requires further exploration to improve evaluations of public health, this project aimed to quantify heavy metal contamination across Chicago's 77 community areas and assess its relationship with socioeconomic and racial demographics. We employed community-based methods to comprehensively survey areas of high human engagement with soil, such as playgrounds, and obtained soil samples from 60 community areas. Concentrations of heavy metals were quantified with Inductively Coupled Plasma-Optical Emission Spectroscopy. Using R and ArcGIS software, these results were geospatially integrated with demographic data from the U.S. Census Bureau and heavy metal regulations from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Holistically, our findings suggested that lower-income and majority non-white Chicago neighborhoods have higher concentrations of heavy metal contamination. Notably, community areas, such as Garfield Park and Brighton Park, consistently exhibited contamination levels that violated EPA thresholds for the majority of metals that were analyzed. Some heavy metals, including arsenic and chromium, exceeded EPA limits across all sampled locations. By elucidating heavy metal contamination patterns, our research highlights communities that are at risk and better informs future environmental policy decisions. Importantly, we emphasized collaborating with communities rather than acting as outside experts, which allows our work to empower communities and support local residents.

title: Therapeutic Targeting of Chromosome Damage in Drug Resistant Brain Cancer
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a deadly brain cancer commonly treated with the chemotherapy drug temozolomide (TMZ), which targets guanine-rich regions of DNA. After TMZ treatment, cancer cells often develop major abnormalities in their nucleus and chromosomes. Normally, chromosome ends, telomeres, are protected by a group of proteins called the shelterin complex, which binds to guanine-rich DNA structures. When this protection is disrupted, it can trigger a telomere crisis, leading to nuclear envelope rupture and a severe form of DNA damage called chromothripsis (CT). Here, we show that TMZ disrupts shelterin binding and increases both nuclear envelope rupture and chromothripsis. We tested the idea that TMZ treatment makes cancer cells more dependent on nuclear transport systems, which move molecules in and out of the nucleus. This dependency may make TMZ-resistant cells more vulnerable to drugs that block nuclear export, such as KPT-330 (Selinexor), which targets the export protein XPO1. To study this, we used DNA sequencing, immunofluorescence, and cell proliferation experiments in both TMZ-sensitive and resistant GBM cells. We also analyzed samples from patients treated with KPT-330. We found that TMZ-resistant cells have shorter telomeres and clear signs of chromothripsis, including nuclear damage and protein mislocalization. These cells were significantly more sensitive to KPT-330 than TMZ-sensitive cells. Importantly, patient data showed reduced chromothripsis markers after treatment, and higher initial levels of these markers were linked to longer survival. Overall, our results suggest that TMZ-induced DNA damage increases reliance on nuclear transport, creating a therapeutic opportunity for targeting resistant GBM with KPT-330.

title: Tunable Permeability of Peptide-Brush-Polymers
abstract: Peptide therapeutics have been in use since the early 20th century, with the advent of insulin. They attach very precisely to important receptors in a human cell that trigger a variety of crucial intracellular effects- this is leveraged to treat metabolic disorders, cardiovascular disease, etc. However, they tend to dissolve in the bloodstream or fail to enter the human cell. Peptide-brush polymers (PBPs) improve on this- they have a tree or brush-like structure that imparts improved stability, with better stability the more hydrophobic their backbone is. However, current literature doesn't describe how this affects permeability- their ability to cross into the human cell. In this project, we wished to investigate this effect through molecular dynamics simulations, a popular computational method. To do so, several model PBPs of varying backbone hydrophobicity and a cell membrane were constructed using the GROMACS software package. Then, the motion through the cell membrane was simulated and the energetic and structural changes characterized. The PBP's repulsion or attraction at relevant coordinates was quantified through weighted histogram analysis method and visualized using the software package Visual Molecular Dynamics. It was found that the greater the hydrophobicity difference between the backbone and side chains, the more difficult it was for the PBP to adapt from the membrane to the aqueous environment. We also wish to further investigate the effect of side chain density. In the future, this may be used to design more permeable and adaptive PBPs.

title: Substrate Temperature Preference During Egg-Laying in Drosophila
abstract: Ectotherms like fruit flies cannot regulate their internal body temperature and instead rely on behavioral strategies to avoid temperatures outside of their optimal range. Unlike adult flies, Drosophila larvae are limited in their ability to escape unfavorable conditions, and thus, female flies have to select a suitable substrate on which to lay eggs to increase the survival of the progeny. However, we know little about the specific choices a female fly makes when choosing the egg-laying substrate. The Gallio Lab studies the molecules and neurons underlying temperature-guided behaviors in Drosophila. In this project, we explored how substrate temperature influences where female fruit flies lay their eggs. We developed a new 2-choice temperature assay in which gravid female flies are given a choice between substrates kept at different temperatures. Using this assay, we found a strong preference for egg laying at 25C over lower or higher temperatures. Surprisingly, the main thermosensory organ of the fly, the antennae, is not required for this behavior. To identify the relevant thermosensory neurons, we have tested the role of candidate cell types using genetic tools to silence their activity. Lastly, we found that Drosophila species adapted to different thermal environments prefer to lay eggs at temperatures matching their native environments. This work suggests the presence of novel thermosensory neurons affecting decision-making during egg-laying behavior in Drosophila.

title: Modeling the Variability in Breast Cancer Resistance Outcomes
abstract: Within a population of genetically identical cancer cells, rare cells can survive drug treatment, leading to relapse in cancer patients. Over the past century, researchers have developed probabilistic models to understand how cancer cells grow. Initial models assumed that all resistant cells were the same, so they modeled them as having the same growth probabilities. Later work introduced additional states like persisters which are slow-proliferating resistant cells, in contrast to fast-proliferating cells. However, with over 20,000 protein-coding genes in DNA, with each acting as a dial that shapes a cell's identity, there are potentially thousands of meaningful states a cell could occupy. Moreover, despite common assumptions, a cell's ability to switch between states, and follow different growth laws, is realistically not governed by a constant probability. Thus, I implemented a theoretical framework that does not require a fixed number of states. Instead, I model a cell's probability to divide or die by drawing the probabilities from a distribution. By treating the probabilities as random variables, I am lifting the assumption that cells follow discrete states. Using my model, I inferred these distributions from publicly available data on breast cancer cells treated with two drugs, a targeted therapy and a chemotherapy. I found that in small doses, the targeted therapy can actually promote cancer cell growth. For both drugs, cells become more volatile at medium doses, making less predictable decisions to divide or die. Lastly, I recovered that the chemotherapy results in greater cell death, which is a known result.

title: Inclusive Writing in the French-speaking World: A Study of Governmental and University Policies in Canada, France, and Belgium
abstract: French inclusive writing (ecriture inclusive) comprises various linguistic strategies-including the feminization of job titles, gender-neutral terminology, and the use of the mid-dot (professeure)-intended to challenge the French-language grammatical convention of the masculine as a universal default. While these practices have gained visibility across the French-speaking world, their official adoption remains inconsistent. This study examines the formal incorporation of inclusive writing practices within governmental and academic institutions in Canada, France, and Belgium, aiming to map the intersection between public policy and institutional implementation. A comparative analysis was conducted using official government documents, including legislative decrees, ministerial circulars, and institutional writing guides, alongside university communication policies and adopted writing guides from each country. It was found that while all three governments broadly support traditional strategies such as feminization and the use of epicene terms, significant restrictions are placed on the mid-dot and neopronouns. A restrictive stance is maintained in France, where inclusive writing has been prohibited in official texts since a 2017 ministerial circular. In Canada, comprehensive guidelines are provided through an interministerial framework, though compliance is voluntary. In Belgium, a supportive 2021 decree was initially adopted, but restrictions regarding the mid-dot have recently been implemented within educational settings. Furthermore, governmental policy is found to correlate with university behavior: French universities exhibit the highest level of restraint, Canadian institutions generally adhere to regional linguistic authority, and Belgian universities demonstrate the most progressive adoption of inclusive forms. These findings highlight the role of governmental policies in shaping institutional inclusive writing practices.

title: Reassessing v-Blockers in HFpEF: Prescribing Patterns And Outcomes In The Cardiometabolic Center Alliance Registry
abstract: Beta-blockers are medications that slow the heart rate and reduce blood pressure, and they are well-established treatments for one form of heart failure where the heart pumps too weakly (HFrEF). However, their benefit is far less certain in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), a distinct and increasingly common condition in which the heart pumps normally but has difficulty relaxing to fill with blood. Despite evolving evidence questioning the routine use of beta-blockers in HFpEF, many patients continue to receive them. To examine this practice, we analyzed data from 620 adults with HFpEF enrolled across 11 clinical sites in the Cardiometabolic Center Alliance (CMCA) registry between March 2019 and May 2025. Beta-blocker use was classified into dosage tiers, and patient characteristics and one-year outcomes - including hospitalizations for heart failure and episodes of fainting - were compared across groups. We found that nearly three-quarters of patients (72.8%) were prescribed beta-blockers, most at moderate doses. Patients with coronary artery disease or atrial fibrillation were more likely to be on them, yet dosing did not consistently reflect recent cardiac events such as heart attacks.
